The path of the established tradition taught by the lineage of excellent gurus beginning with the venerable Somānandanātha.
Having attained its proper form upon the excellent stone [of the mind], the monistic doctrine of Śiva (Īśvarādvaitavāda),

spreading forth from Kashmir with its manifest fragrance and delighting all people of every land, attained a state of universal veneration— unseen in any other region— like the diffusion of saffron. || 1 ||
Cross quickly the ocean of saṃsāra; place your unwavering foot upon the supreme state, which is filled with the bliss of eternal light.
Contemplate the nectar of the realization of non-duality as taught by Śiva.
[It is] that which, by means of its forcefully manifesting and immediate reasoning, causes an internal leaping-up [of realization]. || 2 ||
Oṃ.

Now, in the *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*, [it is said]: Śrīnagara.
First Chapter: Victorious are the rays of the moon of knowledge emerging from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, which are capable of destroying the adversaries of the world’s bliss. (1)
The saviors of those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence, the destroyers of the demon Tāraka—
Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, Sanātana, and Sanandana.
The great sages, Nārada, Agastya, Saṃvarta, Vasiṣṭha, and others,
desiring to know the supreme reality, were directed toward Śiva and Śakti.
Having worshipped him according to the prescribed rite, they, filled with great joy, said to him:
"O Blessed One, we have come seeking the perfection of yoga."
And since that [liberation] cannot occur without yoga, therefore speak of it;
thus was yoga described by those sages who desired it.
Having bowed to Maheśvara, he, with a joyful soul, replied:
"Listen, I shall fully proclaim that which bestows the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments."
The Mālinīvijaya Tantra, which emerged from the mouth of the Supreme Lord, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation; it is the Lord of Umā, worshipped by the immortals. (7)
(2) Goddess Umā, remaining in her own abode, prostrated herself and spoke this:
"The *Siddhayogīśvarītantra*, which extends to ninety million [or, according to another reading, one hundred million] verses."
That which was previously spoken by you, spread across three divisions in the *Mālinīvijaya-tantra* characterized by thirty million verses; (9)
O Maheśvara, the path of yoga has been explained by you in great detail;
furthermore, its summary was likewise taught in twelve [verses]. (Tantra, 10)
Even that extensive work, consisting of thousands [of verses], cannot be grasped by those of small intellect;
therefore, having condensed it, I shall provide here a summary for the benefit of those with limited intelligence. (11)
"O Supreme Lord, out of your grace, tell me that which brings about all accomplishments.
Thus addressed by the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Universe then spoke, smiling.
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the Siddhayogīśvarīmata, which has not been told to anyone, the Mālinīvijayottara. (13)
In the past, I too obtained this from Aghora, the Supreme Self;
it is that which is to be accepted and that which is to be abandoned, to be known according to the ultimate truth.

Śiva, Śakti, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), the Mantras, the Lords of Mantras (Mantreśvaras), and the individual souls (Aṇavas)—this group of six is declared as that which is to be accepted by those seeking the fruit [of liberation]. 15.
Impurity, action, and Māyā—the entire world consisting of Māyā—is said to be entirely to be abandoned; this is the determined reality that must be known. (16)
Having known this and having abandoned [all else], one shall obtain the fruit of all accomplishments.
Therein resides the Lord, the doer of all, the pacifier of all, the omniscient, the master who performs everything. (17)
He is both with parts and without parts, infinite; His power is likewise of that same nature.
Desiring to create the world, at the very beginning of creation, by His own will— || 18 ||
Then Aghora, the supreme Ghoraghora, whose face was of terrible form, awakened eight individuals who were solitary in their consciousness (vijñānakevala). || 19 ||
Bhīma, Bhīṣaṇa, Vamana, and likewise Pivana—
these eight [gods] perform the acts of maintenance, destruction, protection, and grace.

Having then again appointed him to the lordship over the lords of the mantra-maheśvaras (or, according to the *Pañcārthabhāṣya* and *Śrīpūrvaśāstra*, to the lordship over the mantra-īśvara-īśvaras), he likewise created seventy million mantras together with their maṇḍalas.
All these mantras are great-souled and bestow all fruits.
The Self is to be known as fourfold; therein, the Vijñānakevala is one such type.
One joined with *mala* is "engaged in that [limited] action," while one joined with *pralaya* is "isolated in dissolution.
They maintain that *mala* is ignorance, the cause of the sprout of transmigratory existence. (23)
Action, consisting of merit and demerit, is characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth;
by the power of the Lord's will, the desire for its experience arises in this [soul]. (24)
For the sake of accomplishing the means of enjoyment for this one who desires enjoyment, the King of Mantras,
having entered into Māyā with his powers, brought forth the world.

And she is one, all-pervading in nature, and partless (*niṣkalā*)—[according to manuscript *k*: "the nature of the partless"; manuscript *kh* reads "of the partless Śiva-self"]; this passage beginning with "partless" and ending with "is described" is found in manuscript *kh*.
Fulfilled from the book known as Ghasa, she is the treasure of the world;
she is said to be without beginning or end, the sovereign of the auspicious, and free from decay. || 26 ||
She gave birth to Kalā-tattva, through union with which he became a male;
then, having acquired the capacity for agency, he created Vidyā and Rāga.
Knowledge discriminates for him between action and its causes and effects;
attachment, moreover, colors him even toward his own impure enjoyments.
Necessity yokes this individual soul to his own specific karma.
Time also, abiding in its divisions such as the *tuṭi* and so forth, measures this [being]. || 29 ||

From that very principle of *kalā*, he created the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); from that, the qualities (*guṇas*) possessing eightfold power; from those, the intellect (*dhī*); and from the intellect, the ego (*ahaṅkṛta*).
Therein, from that Taijasa [ego], the lord of the senses (the intellect) was born;
from the Vaikarika [ego], the senses arose; and from the third [Tāmasa ego], the subtle elements (tanmātras).
The ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are the organs of perception;
the organs of action are speech, hands, anus, genitals, and feet, respectively. 32.
From the digit (kalā) down to the earth, this entire sphere of saṃsāra—
the whole world beginning with the oceans— revolves by His will.
That very [Lord], who exists as the supreme differentiation of the principles beginning with *kalā* in the form of the worlds (*bhuvana*),
created them for the sake of accomplishing the enjoyment of those who experience worldly existence. (34)
Thus, those persons who abide within this range from *kalā* down to *dharā* should be known as *sakala* (conditioned) by those who desire to destroy that state. (35)
In all three of these states,
being pervaded by both Śiva and Śakti— who possess the nature of concealment— they carry out their various activities.
Thus, throughout the entire world, by virtue of their respective capacities—beginning with those the size of a thumb—there are one hundred and eighteen Rudras. (37)
Having graced them, Śiva himself appointed them to the office of Lords of Mantras;
they, having attained their respective spheres, [serve] those who seek the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. 38.
They bestow upon Brahmā and the others a fruit equal to their own power;
they [bestow it] upon the sages, and those great lords [bestow it] upon the Manvantaras.
They declare that the knowledge of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, as proclaimed by Śiva,
is fully present even at the mere birth of the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.
Three and a half crores of mantras, appointed by Śiva, having shown grace to the multitude of individual souls (aṇus), have gone to the state free from affliction. 41.
Thus, at a certain time, by virtue of his fitness,
this soul becomes connected with the peaceful power of Śiva, which bestows the fruit of liberation.
p.
6) Through connection with that [knowledge], someone is liberated from that very moment;
for some, identity with ignorance ceases. (43)
Pervaded by the power of Rudra and desiring to go forth by the will of Śiva, he is led toward a true guru for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (44)
Having propitiated him and received the initiation of Śaṅkara from him when he is pleased,
one shall go to Śiva either at that very moment, or through enjoyment, or upon the fall of the body. || 45 ||
Having received initiation into yoga and understood it, one should practice yoga;
one attains perfection in yoga and, at its conclusion, the eternal state.
Having attained the supreme state through this sequential yoga,
he does not again fall into the condition of a bound soul (paśu), but abides in his own pure self.
This Self is indeed fourfold, and it is again fourfold;
the Pure Self is enumerated according to the distinctions of the teacher and so forth. (48)
The Guru and the practitioner alike should perform the triad beginning with the daily (nitya) rites;
however, by the command of Śiva, the other two should be performed daily for as long as one lives.
That which is to be accepted and that which is to be rejected has thus been fully proclaimed;
having understood this, the entirety of what is to be known, one shall become solitary for the sake of attaining all perfections. (Or: one shall obtain the fruit of all perfections.
Thus ends the first chapter in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara-tantra. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter:
Now, [we shall describe] these very principles, beginning with earth, in their proper sequence.
This conceptual elaboration is briefly described for the sake of the yogis' attainment of yoga.
The earth-principle (dharātattva) is divided according to the distinction between the possessor of power and its power;
together with its own essential nature (svarūpa), it should be known as fifteenfold.
The possessors of power (śaktimant) are proclaimed to begin with Śiva and end with Sakalātman;
likewise, their powers (śaktis) should be understood by the wise in the same manner. (3)
Thus, this great multitude of principles, beginning with water and ending with the root [Prakṛti],
should be understood as divided by these various distinctions by those who desire its fruit.
By this very same procedure, from the principle of the individual soul (puruṣa-tattva) up to the limit of the principle of limited agency (kalā),
there are thirteen types to be known as the Pralayākalas, just like the Rudras. (5)
In the same way, Māyā is also to be known as ninefold; the Jñānakevalas are likewise [ninefold];
the Mantras are sevenfold; and the Mantranāyakas are fivefold. (6)
The Lords of the Mantreśvaras are threefold, yet Śiva himself is not divided;
this distinction has been described briefly, for it is infinite in its full extent.
In this way, the garland of the worlds (bhuvanamālā), worshipped by yogis for the sake of attaining yogic perfection, is clearly to be understood as divided by these distinctions. (8)
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, whoever knows even one of these principles and worlds, he too shall obtain the fruit of yoga. (9)
Furthermore, he who knows all these principles according to their true nature is declared to be a Guru equal to me, the illuminator of the potency of mantra. (10)
Men who are touched, addressed, or even seen by him with a joyful mind are liberated from the sins committed even throughout seven lifetimes. (11)
Furthermore, those living beings who have been initiated by him and impelled by Śiva attain their desired fruit and go to the state free from all affliction. (12)
The immersion into the power of Rudra is eternally established therein;
and when that exists, one should observe these signs of it. || 13 ||
In this regard, the first sign is unwavering devotion to Rudra; the second is the accomplishment of the mantra, which produces immediate conviction. (14)
Mastery over all sentient beings is known as the third characteristic;
the accomplishment of undertakings already begun they call the fourth sign. (15)
The fifth [sign] to be known is poetic skill, charming and adorned with ornaments;
and the knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises in him spontaneously. (16)
O fair-faced one, the immersion into the power of Rudra is taught to be fivefold,
according to the distinction between the elements, the principles, the self, the lords of mantras, and the powers.
The one designated as the "element" (bhūta) is fivefold; likewise, the other is thirtyfold.
That which is called the "self" (ātman) is said to be threefold, and that designated as "mantra" is tenfold. (18)
This state known as Śakti, though twofold, should be understood in its ultimate sense;
this immersion (samāveśa) is proclaimed to be divided into fifty varieties.
This is declared to be the individual (āṇava) [means], and the empowered (śākta) is likewise remembered as such;
in this way, one should discern that even the divine (śāmbhava) is differentiated by these same divisions.
That immersion which occurs through the visualization of the utterance, the performance, the meditation, the phonemes, and the locations, is correctly called the individual (āṇava) means. || 21 ||
One who, contemplating an object with the mind alone, free from vocal utterance, attains a state of immersion—that is here designated as the Śākta. || 22 ||
The immersion that arises for one who is thinking of nothing at all, through awakening by the Guru, is declared to be the Śāmbhava immersion. (23)
These one hundred divisions have been declared in their proper sequence;
whether in brief or in detail, there is no end to their enumeration.
Wise men should not conceive of any difference in the fruit of realization here;
furthermore, let any other distinction also be understood as it is being stated in brief. (25)

The sequence of all pene trations (āveśa), distinguished by states such as waking and dreaming, is to be fully understood by the wise as fivefold, distinct from its own respective functions— and indeed, distinct from one another. 26.
In that regard, the triad consisting of essential nature (svarūpa), power (śakti), and the "with-parts" (sakala) constitutes this waking state within the fifteenfold division. (27)
In the Ageless (akala), two [states] are to be correctly understood as dream and deep sleep;
the group consisting of the Mantras, their Lords (Mantramaheśvaras), and the Īśvaras is traditionally known as the Fourth (turya). || 28 ||
O fair-faced one, Śakti and Śambhu are to be fully known in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) within the thirteenfold division; both are of the nature of the partless (akala).
The Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and Mantreśānas, as well as Śakti and Śambhu, are proclaimed;
even in the division of the Pralayākala, both [Śakti and Śambhu] belong to the Vijñānakala.
The Mantras, the Lords of Mantras (Mantreśvaras), the Supreme Lords of Mantras (Mantramantreśānas), as well as the Śaktīs and the Lord of Śaktīs (Śaktīśa), are likewise [to be worshipped] as before.
In the ninefold division thus proclaimed, these are one's own Mantras and the Leaders of Mantras.
Their lords, Śakti, and Śambhu are proclaimed as the five states;
likewise, in the sevenfold division, there are the Mantreśas, Īśas, and Śaktis, each belonging to itself.
O lady of excellent complexion, these five alone are to be fully known:
Sva, Śakti, Sanijeśāna, Śakti, and Śambhu within the pentad.
In the triad, one should discern one's own nature as distinct from Śakti, Icchā, and Śiva, by virtue of being the sovereign of their activity and the impeller dependent upon them. (34)

Because of the cessation of desire and because of being established in one's own nature, it is also non-different; thus, in this fivefold division, the object to be known has been proclaimed. So it is said: "In the distinction consisting of the fivefold nature."
Furthermore, the distinction in the designations of these states is revealed:
Piṇḍastha and Sarvatobhadra are considered to be the two names for the waking state (jāgrat). (36)
They maintain that dream has two designations: "abiding in the word" (padastha) and also "pervasion" (vyāpti);
whereas "abiding in form" (rūpastha) is the "great pervasion" (mahāvyāpti), and both of these also belong to deep sleep.
The accumulation that transcends form is correctly designated as the Fourth (turya);
the wise maintain that the Great Accumulation (mahāpracaya) is the state beyond the Fourth (turyātīta). || 38 ||
This distinction has been proclaimed according to the differentiation of individual principles;
for indeed, all principles are contained within these five—listen as follows. (39)
The yoga of those who express the reality of the elements is held to be that which is to be mastered;
they call that "abiding in the body" (piṇḍastha), while others know the other as "abiding in the word" (padastha). || 40 ||
The mantras, their lords, and Śiva are proclaimed as "that which abides in form" (rūpastha);
the supreme power (parā śakti), though active and yet free from affliction, is "beyond form" (rūpātīta).
Free from conceptual proliferation, without appearance, pure, and established in its own self;
Śiva is to be known as that which transcends all, by knowing which one is liberated. (42)

The state of being established in the aggregate (piṇḍastha) is fourfold: impure, purified, awakened, and fully awakened; and the state of being established in the word (padastha) is likewise fourfold. || 43 ||
Going and coming, well-dispersed, gathered, and well-composed—
these four modes of the perception of form should be understood by those who contemplate yoga.
It is arisen, vast, peaceful, and then another which is perfectly serene; it is beyond mind, infinite, the goal of all, and eternally manifest. (45)
"In that accumulation, this one [reality] is to be known as existing within that great [totality].
Thus, the path has been described in five ways; now it is explained in three ways. (46)
The reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is said to extend up to the Vijñānākala; that which ends with Īśvara is known as the principle of Vidya; and they know the remainder to be the state of Śiva.
Thus, the path (adhvan) has been proclaimed there as divided by these distinctions;
now, the simultaneous differentiation of all paths is being described.
The elemental, the primordial, the illusory, and the empowered—thus has this fourfold egg been described in brief. (49)
The two [groups] are distinct and innumerable, each one being separate from the other;
the first is pervaded by the Sustainer (dhārikā), and therein one single reality (tattva) is intended.
One should meditate upon each individual syllable separately,
from the worlds beginning with Kālāgni up to the supreme city of Vīrabhadra, within the words and syllables.
The group of sixteen [principles] is to be known, and the sixfold path has been proclaimed;
by means of the Āpyāyinī [channel], one should perceive the second [group] and the principles therein.
There are twenty-three syllables, the letters beginning with *va* and *ṭ*,
five words, six mantras, and fifty-six cities.
In the fourth [syllable] of the Bodhinī [mudrā], there are seven principles (tattvas) and four cities;
in the third, there are seven phonemes (varṇas), and two pairs of words and mantras.
In the Utpūyinī [kalā], they know there is a fourth; therein one should perceive three principles (tattvas), three phonemes (varṇas), one mantra, and one word (pada). || 55 ||
One should know that, in brief, there are eighteen worlds.
The supreme Śiva-tattva is the ultimate peace; therein, Kalā provides space.
One should discern the sixteen vowels as the mantra and the single word;
thus, the sixfold path has been briefly proclaimed.
Since the entire world, both pure and impure, originates from the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
therefore everything is held to be pure by means of these pure cosmic eggs.
O lady of virtuous vows, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Īśvara—these four Lords should be understood as distinct within these [forms], yet they are peaceful. (59)
For whoever is superior in qualities compared to another is said to be above that person.
All this has been told to you; what else do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the second chapter, on Pervasion, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter: Thus addressed by the one who brings joy to the world, the Great Goddess—
Having prostrated, he spoke these words again to the Lord of the World.
Thus it is, O Mahādeva; it has been declared otherwise not at all.
Just as it was told, so has it been understood from the beginning in its proper sequence.
O Supreme Lord, I now desire to hear the designations for the forms of Śiva and other entities; by Your grace, You should deign to speak of them.
Thus addressed by Maheśānī, Hara, the remover of the world's affliction,
spoke the mantras that have come down through the lineage of oral tradition.
O Goddess, that power of the Creator of the universe which has been described as inherent (samavāyinī) becomes His will when He desires to emit [the world]. || 5 ||
Listen to how even that which is single comes to possess multiplicity;
it should be understood with absolute certainty that "it is thus" and not otherwise. (6)
When it makes known that "this object is thus" or "let this entire universe become thus," being oriented toward action, it is called the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) here in this world. (7)
15) That which, having arisen at that very moment, performs various corresponding actions, is here called "action" (*kriyā*).
Thus, although this very [action] is of two forms, it further attains multiplicity through its divisions.
[The state of] infinity through its various divisions. || 8 ||
Under the influence of the limiting adjuncts of objects, the Sovereign Lady (Īśvarī) becomes like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
Having first entered therein into the state of the subject (mātṛbhāva), she then differentiates that state of subjectivity.
The Mālinī is twofold, ninefold, and indeed fiftyfold;
it is twofold due to the distinction between the nature of seed-syllables (bīja) and matrices (yoni). The vowels are considered to be the seed-syllables.
And the Yoni is remembered as ninefold through the division of the groups beginning with *ka*;
by the differentiation of each individual letter, it shines with fifty rays. (11)
In this context, Śiva is designated as the seed (bīja) and Śakti as the womb (yoni);
indeed, every power of Śambhu is celebrated as the expressive [agent] (vācaka). (12)
The group of eight here should be known as beginning with Aghora in due order;
that same group, through the differentiation of their powers (śakti), is the group of eight beginning with Māheśvarī.
Māheśī, Brāhmaṇī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Aindrī, Yāmyā, Cāmuṇḍā, and Yogīśī—these are considered [the eight Mātṛkās]. || 14 ||
O fair-faced one, they were fashioned by the Supreme Lord as the designators of those Rudras, who are divided into fifty varieties and numbered accordingly.
In that very same way, I shall describe the number and sequence of those powers, as well as their entire classification; listen to it as I speak. (16)
He is the immortal one, filled with immortality, appearing as nectar, and flowing as nectar;
he is a flood of nectar, a wave of nectar, and another who is a chariot of nectar.
He whose limbs are nectar, whose body is nectar, and who indeed utters nectar;
he whose mouth is nectar, whose form is nectar, and likewise he who sprinkles nectar. || 18 ||
Tanmūrti, Amṛteśa, and another, Sarvāmṛtadhara—
these sixteen are declared to have originated from the seed-syllable of Rudra.
Jaya, Vijaya, Jayanta, Aparājita, Sujaya, Jayarudra, Jayabhadra, Jayakīrti, and Jayāvaha. || 20 ||
The embodiment of victory, the enthusiasm for victory, the giver of victory, the increaser of victory;
the strong, the exceedingly strong, Balabhadra, and the bestower of strength. (21)
He who brings strength, the powerful one, the giver of strength, the lord of strength;
the delighter, auspicious in every way, the embodiment of auspiciousness, and the bestower of well-being. || 22 ||
Sumanas, Spṛhaṇa, Durgā, Bhadrakāla, Manonuga, Kauśika, Kālaviśveśa, Suśiva, and Kopa. || 23 ||
These thirty-four, born from the womb, are proclaimed;
having come under the influence of the female recitation, these alone are the Śaktis here. (24)
(17) Arising from the source of the seed-syllables and resting upon the power of Rudra,
there is no exhaustive enumeration because the expressive words are infinite. || 25 ||
By means of this [scripture], which contains the essence of all treatises,
the Supreme Lord, according to his own will, awakened Aghora.
Fully awakened by her, the Lord, having agitated the womb with his powers,
created the phonemes (varṇas) which possessed sounds identical to hers and were equal in number to them.
Embraced by those various [deities], O Goddess worshipped by heroes, they become bestowers of the fruits of all desires for the foremost of practitioners; it is not otherwise. (28)
By them this entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans, is pervaded;
from them the scriptures and the Vedas arise again and again. (29)
O Great Goddess, although the differentiation of the great-souled power of Śiva is infinite, it is declared to be threefold according to the differentiation of its effects.
Those others, known as the most terrible (ghoratara), are said to embrace the rudra-aṇus and cause the individual souls (aṇus) who are completely absorbed in sense objects to fall lower and lower.
Those [impurities] which, as before, produce attachment to the fruits of mixed karma and obstruct the path to liberation, are the terrible *parāpara* [impurities]. (32)
As before, those supreme Aghora Śiva-powers, which bestow the fruit of the abode of Śiva upon the multitude of living beings, have been described by the knowers of that [reality]. (33)
p.
18) Just as all these [powers] abide, even when established within the aggregate of all atoms, so have they been described; O Śambhu, the power of Śaṅkara is indeed one alone. 34.

Another distinction of this [goddess] based on the difference of her designators will now be explained for the sake of the successful attainment of desired fruits by those who follow the Mantras and Tantras. (35)

In ritual acts of deposition (*nyāsa*) that lack specific injunctions, the knower of mantras should perform the *mālinī* [deposition], which has distinct origins, for the sake of the body of Śakti. (36)

The letter *śa* is the tuft of hair, *ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ* is the garland on the head, *tha* is the forehead, *ca* and *dha* are the eyes, *ī* is the nose, *u* and *ū* are the ears, and *ṇu* and *ṇū* are the two oceans.
The letters *va*, *ka*, *va*, *i*, and *ā* are located in the mouth, teeth, tongue, and speech;
*va* and *bha* are in the throat and the shoulders beginning with the right; and *ḍa* and *ḍha* are in the two arms. (38)

Ṭha and tha are in the two hands; jha and ña are the fingers; jra and ṭa are the trident and skull-bowl; pa and ha are the chest; cha and la are the breasts; mā is the milk; and that living soul (jīva) is joined with the visarga.

The vital breath (prāṇa) situated in the heart is said to be followed by those [consonants] starting with ta; [the letters] ṣa and kṣa reside in the belly and the navel; [the letters] ma, śa, and ṇa reside in the hips, the private parts, and the pair of thighs; and likewise, [the letter] ja resides in the knees.
The letters *e* and *ai* are likewise the shanks; the letters *ta* and *pa* are the feet.
From these, the Vidyās and Mantras are to be extracted; listen as they are explained. (41)
Then one should fashion the word with the right shank accompanied by a bindu;
likewise, the fourth [syllable] is the tooth joined with the shank.

The staff joined with the right knee, the vital breath (prāṇa) joined with the staff situated [therein], and the two staffs of the teeth, located separately at the heart, the staff, and the waist, as before. (43)
Then, having extracted the *u* standing with the *bindu*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the tooth as before,
one should again extract the staff alone, accompanied by the left-hand mudrā. (44)
One should place the heart joined with the right knee and the vital breath (prāṇa) joined with the individual self (jīvātman);
then, having performed the placement of the teeth as before, one should likewise place the staff alone.
The buttock joined with the right thumb, the second [toe] with the tongue,
the tooth along with the nose, the peak of the right [hand], and then the buttock alone.
Again, in the same manner, one should place the *śikhara*, then the *jaṭhara* alone;
then the ear joined with the right knee, and the throat alone. (47)
Placing only the buttocks on the ground, joining the heart with the tongue,
and lifting only the face, one should direct the vital breath (prāṇa) toward the first knee.
There is also a set of four tridents and staffs; of these, the first two are positioned standing upright.
At the end of that [first pair], one should place a skull resting on its left foot.
Then, from Paramaghora up to Pādyaka and so forth, it is as before;
she is called Parāparā, and Aparā is now described.
First, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) ending with Aghora; then again, the vital breath (prāṇa) joined with the Bindu.
Having performed the placement accompanied by the Vāmā mudrā, one offers the water for the feet (pādya) as before using the letters beginning with Ka.
This is declared to be the "other" [form]; now hear of the supreme Rudra-śakti.
The mantras come face to face [with their power] by the mere utterance of them. || 52 ||
The slender body trembles and there is a sudden leaping up; there is the binding of mudrās, singing, and even the howling of jackals. (53)
One may perform the narration and so forth of past and future events;
such is the living soul (jīva), accompanied by the left shank, which has come down through the lineage of succession.
This accomplishment, which bestows the fruit of all desires, has been transmitted by me;
it must never be given to one who is not a disciple, nor ever to one who lacks devotion.
O fair-faced one, that which is to be given should be bestowed upon him who beholds with devotion this triad as equal: Rudra, Rudra-śakti, and the Guru. (56)
The disciple, too, should receive [the teaching] only when the guru has been fully satisfied by means of his body, material offerings, pure knowledge, ritual actions, virtues, and so forth. (57)
But when she has been awakened by that preceptor with a joyful heart, then she should be known as the bestower of accomplishment, and not otherwise, O goddess worshipped by heroes. (58)
The eight yoginīs of great power, born from the limbs of the higher and lower [deities], consist respectively of five, six, five, four, two, three, and two syllables. (59)
The seven [syllables] are to be known as having eleven phonemes, joined with one and a half phonemes each;
the *jīva* [syllable] is endowed with the six long vowels and distinguished by its respective class (*jāti*). || 60 ||
The limbs of the triple Vidyā consist of the short vowels; with five *oṃ*s as the faces, the mantra becomes the heart of the limbs of the Vidyā. (61)
"Oṃ amṛte tejomālini svāhā"— these words, adorned with [the syllable] 'da',
consisting of eleven syllables, are declared to be the Brahmaśiras, O Dear One. (62)
The eight-syllable Rudrāṇī mantra, beginning with the Praṇava (Oṃ) and ending with "hūṃ phaṭ," should be known as the Śikhā-vidyā of the group of sciences. || 63 ||
The eleven-syllable armor-mantra, beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*, addressed to Vajrin and Vajradhara, is known as "Puruṣṭuta. || 64 ||
Ślīpada, the word *paśu*, and [the mantra] beginning with *bhava* and ending in *hūṃ phaṭ*—
this is declared to be the supreme Pāśupata, consisting of six and a half syllables. (65)
The wise one should visualize Indra and the other deities with long vowels, accompanied by the *sū* (the nasal bindu), and their weapons with short vowels.
In the same way, Viṣṇu and Prajāpati are to be conceived by means of the nose and the milk;
however, the first and third *svaras* (vowels) are the designators of the lotus and the discus.
Thus has the group of Mothers (or: the group of mantras) been proclaimed, which bestows the fruit of all desires;
for the sake of the yogic accomplishment of yogins, what else do you wish to ask? 68.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the Extraction of Mantras, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Then, having heard this, the sages, their eyes filled with joy, [listened].
Having bowed down to the slayer of Krauñca, they spoke these words once more: || 1 ||
When asked by the Goddess regarding the procedure for the path of yoga, the Supreme Lord, having made a formal promise, spoke: "For what purpose is the definition of mantra? (2)
Thus addressed by them, the high-minded Kārttikeya spoke these words to them for the purpose of dispelling their doubts.

They maintain that the conjunction of one entity with another entity is what is called "the object to be known" (jñeya), for the purpose of establishing its status as something to be abandoned and so forth. (4)
Even that knowledge, though it has two forms, cannot be known without [the means];
for its establishment, the knowledge described by Śiva has been set forth. (5)
The characteristics of mantra are also sufficient for the complete accomplishment of yoga with seed;
yet there is no eligibility for the Yoga of Śaṅkara without initiation (dīkṣā).
And that [wisdom] is said to be twofold through the distinction between action and knowledge;
it must be practiced in those two ways, and for that reason this has been illustrated.
And by this [initiation], there is not only eligibility for yoga;
rather, through Śiva-initiation, there is also eligibility for mantra and liberation.
O best of sages, having heard these words of her husband, Ambā, her body bristling with horripilation, spoke these words again: (9).
Within the body of Abhinnamālinī, the principles (tattvas), the worlds (bhuvanas),
the limited powers (kalās), the words (padās), and the mantras have been correctly ascertained.
O Lord, tell me how these [deities] are situated within the body of that Mālinī of mine, whose origin you have described as distinct.
Thus addressed by the Great Goddess, Bhairava, the bestower of abundant enjoyments,
illuminated the quarters of space with the radiance of shimmering moonbeams.
He whose command is cherished by the garlands upon the crests of the foremost gods and demons spoke these sweet words, which were intended to dispel the Lord’s distress.
O Goddess, regarding that Mālinī of diverse origins whom I have described,
I shall now explain everything concerning its constituent parts exactly as they exist.

The earth element has been indicated in due order at the end of the letter *da*; one should perceive the twenty-three principles, beginning with the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and ending with primordial matter (*pradhāna*). || 15 ||
In the first group of seven beginning with *ṭha*, there are seven [categories] starting with *puruṣa*, as before.
One should know that among the *iṅghas* there are three; from knowledge (*vidyā*) up to the complete limit (*sakalāvadhi*).
Within the Śiva-tattva, one should perceive sixteen [elements] beginning with the letter *ga* and ending with *na*:
the kalās, the words, the mantras, and the worlds, O beautiful lady. (17)
They are to be understood as before, according to the distinctions of their respective numbers;
listen now to how they are divided according to the three branches of knowledge.
In the Niṣkala [state], there are two: the single-syllable *pada* and the pair consisting of the three-syllable and the single-syllable.
In the Sakala [state], however, one should know that there are two pairs of five-syllable [units]. (19)
Two [mantras] consisting of four and one syllable each are considered to belong to the triad beginning with Māyā;
and one consisting of four syllables is considered to belong to the dyad beginning with Kāla.
In the *rañjaka* [kalā], two syllables are taught; in the *pradhāna*, three syllables are desired.
In the *buddhi*, due to the pervasion of the eight deities, a word of two syllables is desired. (21)
Then, by the pervasion of five groups of eight, there are four mantra-words consisting of two, one, two, and two syllables respectively,
while the fifth consists of one and a half syllables.
In the earthly principle (tattva), there are three syllables and a half for each [of the consonants k,
kh, g]; however, in the limbs of Parā, all else— the phonemes, mantras, kalās, and so forth— is present.
Two eggs are pervaded by [the first power] together with half [a unit], while each of the other two is pervaded separately;
this pervasion of the lower [power] is declared to be in reverse order.
The three eggs are pervaded by the letter *sā*, the fourth by the trident (*triśūla*);
that which transcends all is pervaded by the emission (*visarga*)—this is held to be the pervasion of Parā. (25)
All this must be fully understood by the yogin who desires the welfare of himself or others; otherwise, that [welfare] is not attained. (26)
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, only two are to be known as givers of liberation: the man of knowledge and the yogi.
Because of their distinctness therein, this must be understood by those who desire the fruit.

Knowledge is said to be threefold; among these, the first is held to be that consisting of hearing (śruta), then that consisting of reflection (cintā-maya), and finally that consisting of cultivation (bhāvanā-maya). (28)

The thorough comprehension of the meaning of the treatise is considered the learning of one who is distracted; it consists of knowing, "This is here," "That is there," and "This is applicable in this case. (29)
Having thoroughly examined the meaning of the treatises as established in their proper sequence, knowledge consisting of reflection (cintāmaya-jñāna) is taught to be of two kinds. (30)
There, [the knowledge] is divided into "sluggish" and "well-practiced. Among these, the "well-practiced" is described as follows:
when that [knowledge] is perfectly accomplished, there arises that which consists of meditative cultivation (bhāvanāmaya). || 31 ||
Since the yogi, having attained yoga, obtains the fruit of yoga, the knower (jñānin) is thus declared to be fourfold according to the distinction of his realization. || 32 ||
O Goddess, the yogi is of four kinds— namely, the beginner (saṃprāpta), the striving (ghaṭamāna), the perfected (siddha), and the most perfected (siddhatama)— and he proceeds accordingly.

Yoga is declared to be threefold, like the description of immersion (*samāveśa*). Among these, that which consists of having received the instruction through the sequence of oral tradition (*pāramparya*)— // 34 //
That one who has attained yoga should be known by the wise as being of three kinds:
the repeated rejoining of the mind that has strayed from reality. (35)
The wise desire that which one performs while striving;
with the mind, one holds fast to that alone and not to anything else as a second.
Then he should be known as a Siddhayogin by those seeking the fruit of yoga—[the one] who, moreover, remains exactly as he is, wherever he may be situated. (37)
(26) While enjoying its fruit, he is by no means deprived of it;
O Dear One, he should be known as one who is perfectly accomplished and equal to Sadāśiva. (38)
The progressive superiority of these [categories] has been declared:
among both the possessors of knowledge (jñānins) and the practitioners of yoga (yogins), the one perfected in yoga is the most excellent. (39)
For he possesses knowledge that is free from the fruits of prior yoga, and because he is declared by the wise to be a bestower of liberation through his well-practiced knowledge. (40)
All this has been told, O you who are worshipped by yogis; having summarized the meaning of the tantra, it is taught in brief for the benefit of yogis. 41.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth section. Now, therefore, O Īśvarī, I shall fully explain the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan).
First, the world of Kālāgni must be purified with diligent effort.
Avīci, Kumbhīpāka, and Raurava as the third—when the world of the Kūṣmāṇḍas is purified, all are purified; of this there is no doubt. (2)
Then there are the seven netherworlds (pātālas); at their beginning is Mahātala, then Rasātala, and beyond that Talātala.
Sutala, Nitala, Vitala, and Talātala—by means of pure hāṭaka (gold), the purification of all these is desired. || 4 ||
Beyond that, the earth should be known as consisting of seven continents and oceans;
in its center stands Mount Meru, the abode of the gods.
The world of earth (Bhūrloka), and above that the world of heaven (Svarloka), and above that [are] Mahas, Janas, Tapas, and Satya; this is the sevenfold world-system.
Therein, the fourteen-fold collection of living beings proceeds:
the stationary, the serpent species, and likewise the bird species, and others.
The one known as Mṛga, the one called Paśu, the fifth which is another, the human (Mānuṣa), the Paiśāca, the Rākṣasa, the Yākṣa, the Gāndharva, and the Aindra. || 8 ||
The Saumya, the Prājāpatya, and the Brāhma—these fourteen [purifications] are for this entire [ritual];
when the Brāhma purification has been accomplished, there is the complete purification of all this. (9)
The world belongs to Viṣṇu; therefore, that which follows it is mine.
In that pure state, everything becomes pure; of this there is no doubt. || 10 ||
O Dear One, by these five pure worlds beginning with Kālāgni,
all this that is situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) becomes purified.
Outside of that, one should subsequently purify the ten separate worlds of the hundred Rudras, which are surrounded by their respective leaders.
Ananta is the first among them, and Kapālīśa is another;
likewise Agnirudra, Yama, Nairṛta, and Bala. (13)
Śīghra, Nidhīśvara, and another, Sarvavidyādhipa; Śambhu, Vīrabhadra, and Vidhūmajvalanaprabha. (14)
By these ten, numbered as one, a hundred pure [units] is considered pure;
above them, five groups of eight are situated in front.
Lakulī, Bhārabhūti, Diṇḍi, Āṣāḍhi, and Puṣkara;
as well as Naimiṣa, Prabhāsa, and Amareśa—these constitute the group of eight.
This group of eight Pātyas has been declared; it is more secret than the secret.
Among them, Bhairava, Kedāra, and Mahākāla are situated together with Madhyamā. (17)
Āmrātikeśa, Jalpeśa, Śrīśaila, along with Harīndu;
Bhīmeśvara, Mahendra, Ādṛha, and Vimaleśvara. (18)
Kanakhala, Nakhala, Kurukṣetra, and likewise Gayā—
this third secret [place] is now declared to be pure. (19)
Sthāṇu and Svarṇākṣaka are the first; Bhadra and Gokarṇaka are the next two;
then Mahākāla, Avimukteśa, Rudrakoṭi, Ambara, and Āpada. (20)
Sthūla, Sthūleśvara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Kālañjara, Maṇḍaleśvara, Mākoṭa, Diraṇḍa, and Chagalāṇḍaka. (21)
The eight Sthāṇus are said to exist up to the limit of the ego (ahaṃkāra);
now hear from me as I describe the eight classes of divine beings (devayoni) situated in the intellect (buddhi). || 22 ||
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, and Aindra, as well as the Saumya, the Prājāpatya, and the Brāhma is desired as the eighth. (23)
The *Yogāṣṭaka* was not composed there at the beginning regarding the Pradhāna;
rather, the *Vaibhava*, *Brāhma*, and *Vaiṣṇava* were composed immediately after that. (24)
The eightfold yoga consists of Kaumāra, Auma, and Śrīkaṇṭha; likewise, within Puruṣa are Vāma, Amogha, Ugra, Bhaveśāna, and Ekavīra.
Pracaṇḍa, Umādhava, and Āja; then Ananta and Ekaśiva;
Krodheśa and Caṇḍa in the Vidyā [tattva]; and Saṃvarta and Jyotis. (26)
In the principle of Kalā, the two destroyers of the five gods (the Rudras) are to be fully known;
Ekavīra, Śikhaṇḍīśa, and Śrīkaṇṭha are those who have resorted to Kāla.
Mahātejas and the others, known as the lords of the mandalas, reside there in the Māyā-tattva; among them are Vāmadeva and Bhavodbhava. (28)
Led by Ekapiṅga, Iṣāna, and Bhuvaneśa,
they were accompanied by Aṅguṣṭhamātra and possessed a splendor equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
The wise say that there are five worlds even within the principle of Vidyā;
among them, the first is Hālāhala Rudra, and the next is Krodha.
Ambikā, Aghorā, and Vāmadevī are proclaimed;
in Īśvara, there are the worlds beginning with Pibanā and ending with Aghorā,
which are the Maheśvaras.
Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā, as well as Śakti and Sadāśiva—these five worlds in the Sakala state are known by the wise. (32)
Thus, among all the principles (tattvas), one hundred and eighteen worlds are to be fully known; this is stated in brief, and not in detail.
By means of this purity, all things are purified without a doubt;
indeed, O Great-Minded One, when the purification of all paths is to be performed, [this is the means]. (34)
Having thoroughly purified the Sakala state, one should establish union with Śiva;
the knower of Yoga, desiring enjoyment, should meditate upon the Sakala and perform Yoga.
Thus has this path of the world been proclaimed according to my doctrine.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on the Path of the Worlds (*bhuvanādhvā*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
Now begins the sixth chapter:
Now, [we shall explain] how this collection of entities is established within the body.
It is performed during the initiations of knowledge; thus it is now being declared.
One should place the five elements beneath the feet with a pervasion of two finger-breadths;
then, one should place the earth-principle up to the ankles, and so forth, in successive order.
In the same manner, above that,

one should contemplate the group of six principles (tattva-ṣaṭka) ending with the conclusion of the sixth stage, from the principle of the Person (puruṣa-tattva) up to the principle of Limited Agency (kalā-tattva).
Then, being well-composed, one should meditate upon the four principles beginning with Māyā, extending through the entire range up to Sakala by means of a pervasion of four finger-breadths.
Thereafter, one should contemplate the Śiva-principle, which is of the nature of light and undisturbed,
pervading all things both externally and internally.
This assignment [of mantras] has been proclaimed according to the division of the thirty-six principles;
now, the five principles are described as they exist within the body.
From the navel upwards, there are six successive joints (as stated in the *Tantrāloka*:
"the first six joints").
The region up to the ankles is pervaded by the earth principle (*dharātattva*), while the remainder here is pervaded by water (*ambu*).
And twenty-two joints above that are enveloped by fire;
from there, twelve joints are declared to be pervaded by air. (8)
One should meditate upon that which extends to the end of space, the supreme peace, the all-pervading [reality].
This is likewise intended in the ritual procedures for the five sections beginning with Śakti on the path. (9)
In the three sections up to the throat, the Ātmatattva is declared;
above that is the Vidyātattva, while the Śivatattva is as before.
Thus the procedure for the reality has been declared; now the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is likewise described.
From Kālāgni up to Vīrabhadra, there are sixteen cities.
One should place [the mantras], having meditated upon them in the proper sequence as prescribed, extending up to the ankles;
from there, one should proceed in order starting from Lakulīśa, with an extension of one finger-breadth for each.
One should place [the deities] up to Dviraṇḍa; Chagalāṇḍaka occupies three finger-breadths.
Then, according to the extent of a quarter-finger-breadth, one should separately place the eight deities of Yoga.

Then, by an extension of half a finger-breadth from that as well, one should contemplate the six cities in sequence; then the fourfold group in two [locations], and finally the single [city] in one [location].
In the triad beginning with Vidyā, there are two, one, and one division respectively, starting from the north;
each one is taught in due order according to time.
The pervasion of the lords of the maṇḍalas is considered to be half a finger-breadth;
for the triad above that, it is known as being less than three parts of a joint.
But for the second [type], a complete pentad has been proclaimed;
one should likewise observe another as an octad and a pentad. || 17 ||

33) In this procedure for the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan), one should contemplate Śiva as before; here, the planes (padāni) are of two kinds, distinguished by the categories (varga) and the vidyās. 18.
Listen now to how their pervasion by those mantras occurs, just as it does at present:
the first [space] is four finger-breadths, while the other two are each eight finger-breadths.
From one [of these], there are ten finger-breadths; thus, fifteen finger-breadths.
Another, the ninth, is great and all-pervasive, being increased by four.
In the nineteen-fold division, the pervasion of the words is stated:
each [subsequent word] should be known as two finger-breadths, and prior to that are three words.
Seven finger-breadths [in the *Tantrāloka* it says eight finger-breadths], then four, and ten finger-breadths beyond that;
two finger-breadths, and two other steps, and six finger-breadths beyond that. (22)
Another [part] is twelve finger-breadths long; two others are five finger-breadths each separately.
There are two feet, each with four joints; two are at the front, and two are separate from that.
Another pervasive state has also been proclaimed as that [state];
this other method has been declared. Now hear the doctrine of the Supreme-Non-Supreme (Parāpara). || 24 ||
As before, the earth element is to be known as four finger-breadths;
one should mark the elements ending with intellect (dhiṣaṇā) as being two and a half finger-breadths each.
The primary [element] should be known as three finger-breadths; the remainder should be indicated as before.
In the subsequent [elements] also, the earth is as before, and the others are likewise three finger-breadths each. || 26 ||
The primary [element] consists of four joints (*catuṣparva*), and one should rely on the remainder as previously described.
For the sixfold division of the phonemes (*varṇa*) is said to be twofold.
is accepted. || 27 ||
It should be known in its ultimate sense through the method of the path of reality, according to the sequence of the previous sūtras regarding the stages, mantras, kalās, and so forth. || 28 ||

One should perform the threefold state according to the path described for the letters of the principles; thus, by the Guru, who is the very form of Śiva, [the initiation] of the one whose body has become such [is performed].
Initiation, which bestows all fruits, must be performed according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the Path of the Body, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. 6.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the powers of Śiva known as mudrās.
By means of which [and by those which are indeed pure], when the practitioner is well protected, he shall attain the accomplishment of the mantra. || 1 ||
The trident, as well as the lotus, the spear, the discus together with the thunderbolt, the staff, the fangs, the great ghost, the great mudrā, and Khageśvarī. (2)

Mahodayā and Karālā [hold] a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) together with a skull-cup (kapāla), a plow (hala), a noose (pāśa), a goad (aṅkuśa), a bell (ghaṇṭā), a mallet (mudgara), and another [weapon], a trident (triśikha). || 3 ||
Āvāha, sthāpanī, nirodhā, dravyadā, and nati—these, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, are to be known as Amṛtā and Yogamudrā. (4)
The index, middle, and ring fingers of the right hand are extended;
when the little finger and thumb are pressed together, this is proclaimed as the trident (triśūla) mudrā.
Having formed the hands into the shape of a lotus, one should display the lotus mudrā;
having made the two hands face each other and extended, with the fingers interlaced.
When the middle finger is extended at the joint, it is considered the Śakti of Kaumārī;
[it is formed] from the right hand with the left fist turned upward.
One should place the right hand facing downwards above the left hand which is turned upwards.
The little finger and the thumb joined together, with the remaining fingers resting at the wrist—this is known as the Vajra-mudrā; it belongs to Indra and brings about satisfaction. (9)
The right fist extended upwards with the thumb placed inside is renowned as the Staff Mudrā (daṇḍamudrā), which is dear to the family of Vaivasvata.
One should extend the little finger of the left fist toward the mouth;
O Goddess, this is proclaimed as the fang-mudrā, the delight of the Cāmuṇḍā family.
The foot is placed upon the left knee, the hands hang down behind the back,
the eyes are distorted, the neck is bent, and the tongue is protruded.
She is beloved by the entire host of yogis and is considered the delighted Mistress of Yogis (Yogīśvarī).
The wise practitioner should bring his two hands, palms facing downward, from the feet up to the heart. 13.
One should lead the two [fingers] facing upwards from the ends of the faces directed crosswise;
this is renowned as the Mahāmudrā for the rite of purifying the body. (14)
And this [practice] performs all actions for the sake of the yogis' attainment of yoga.
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), the yogi should place the Lord of the Eye (Akṣeśvara) at the navel.
One should lead that state into the form of a staff until it reaches the three voids;
having restrained it there, one should swiftly impel it through the three voids.
Having bound this, the great hero attains the power of moving through the sky:
the right hand is turned downward and the left is turned upward with the palm facing up. (17)
One should press his ring finger and middle finger with the left thumb;
likewise, one should press the little finger with the forefinger and the forefinger with the little finger. (18)
One should press the thumb with the middle and ring fingers;
this is the mudrā called Mahodayā, which brings great prosperity to human beings. || 19 ||
With the ring finger and the little finger,
the practitioner of mantra should tear open the corners of the mouth, move the tongue, and utter the sound "hā hā."
This fierce mudrā, which causes fear to the wicked, possesses a wrathful gaze;
the left fist is placed upon the left shoulder with the index finger raised.
The mudrā known as Khaṭvāṅga has been described; now hear about the Kapāla.
The right palm is concave, with the fingers slightly contracted [or: slightly bent]. || 22 ||
The skull is thus to be understood; now the plow is described:
[it is formed] by the left fist grasping the index finger of the right clenched fist. (23)
When the two index fingers are bent and grasped [by the fist], it is known as the *halamudrā*.
With the fists of the right and left hands, the two index fingers [are extended] from the backs. (24)
The noose is formed by the left thumb-tip joined to the extended and slightly bent [forefinger];
the left fist is like a plough, while the goad is likewise [formed] without the right hand. (25)
When the left hand is positioned face-downward, the wise one should move the right index finger situated in the middle; this is considered the beloved Ghaṇṭāmudrā.
The two hands should be made facing upwards with the fingers interlaced;
the two index fingers should rest upon the middle phalanges of the ring fingers at their base-joints. (27)

The two middle fingers [in their own middle] should be joined even though they are rough; the two little fingers should also be joined up to the knuckles. The two index fingers, situated on the sides of the middle fingers, should be arranged so as to be slightly separated.
This mudgara and triśikha [or triśira] indeed cause possession in an instant;
having formed an añjali with both hands, [the thumbs] should be placed upon the root joints of the ring fingers. (29)
The wise one should form two thumbs in the rite of invoking with mantras;
the mudrā known as Sthāpanī consists of two fists with the thumbs raised.
The two thumbs entering the womb are to be known as Saṃnirodhinī;
Dravyadā is declared to be [the one] facing directly toward that. 31.
With the two hands joined palm-to-palm at the heart with fingers extended,
this is the *namaskṛti* mudrā for the rite of saluting the mantra.
The fingers of both hands should be placed so that they mutually interlock;
one should join the right little finger to the tip of the left ring finger.
Likewise, with the right [hand] and the left, the index and middle fingers [are joined], and the two thumbs are placed at the base of the middles; this is the Amṛtaprabhā mudrā. (34)
(39) The right [hand] is placed at the base of the navel, positioned above the left;
the index finger and thumb are joined and raised for the rite of yoga. (35)
In this manner, the wise mantra-practitioner should bind the collection of mudrās at his heart;
the expression for all of them is "Oṃ Hrīṃ [Name] Tatas Namaḥ. (36)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on Mudrās, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sacrifice that grants all desires.
By the mere sight of whom one becomes esteemed by the Yoginīs. || 1 ||
There, first of all, one should cause a beautiful sacrificial ground to be constructed in an auspicious field,
provided with a circular fire-pit (agni-kuṇḍa).
It should have twenty-five joints all around, with a navel reaching halfway up;
it should be adorned with a belt occupying one-fourth of its circumference and with well-beautified joint-lips.

Then, having bathed and conquered the pairs of opposites through the bath of inner disposition (bhāva), the knower of mantras performs that which is declared to be sixfold, beginning with the sequence of the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna).
Having consecrated the ashes seven times with the Great Weapon mantra,
one should dust the body with them in the order of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama) for the purpose of cleansing impurities through the ash-bath.
Thereafter, one should veil the head and other parts with the five ancillaries of knowledge (vidyāṅga).
One should then perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) using the six-limbed root mantra itself [or, according to manuscript k, using water].
Then, whether unclothed or well-clothed, one should wash one's hands and feet;
having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the purification (mārjana) with the Vidyā consisting of many syllables.
Having performed the general ritual placement (nyāsa), one should perform the Aghamarṣaṇa rite with the second [verse],
the worship with the Mālinī, and recite the supreme single-syllabled mantra.
Even when bathing in water, one should touch the body as before with earth consecrated seven times with the Astra-mantra and perform the impurity-bath (malasnāna). (9)
And here, the ritual bathing and other rites are as before, but with water;
having performed the ordinary ritual bath, one should [use] water consecrated by the threefold mantra of the Vidyās.
The knower of mantras should pour water upon his head for the purpose of the mantra-bath;
or, by means of dust raised by a cow's tail, he should perform the Vāyavya bath.
Uttering the great mantra, he should proceed seven steps while absorbed in meditation;
then, recollecting the supreme and the non-supreme, he should return to that very same place.
Even a divine [image] is considered to be of such a nature through contact with rain and heat;
however, in that case, the practitioner should contemplate the supreme nectar flowing [from it]. (13)
Having raised the fire from the base of the thumb with the Astra-mantra, one should burn [the impurities];
thereafter, one should drench one's own body with the supreme nectar.
Taking up the mantra from the sun and other sources, one should go while recollecting the weapon-mantra (astra);
purified by the weapon-mantra, one should enter the sacrificial hall, pure and undisturbed.
There, having worshipped the door-keepers, one should cast a flower consecrated with the Great Weapon mantra while meditating on it as blazing, for the pacification of obstacles.
Then, having performed the ritual visualization of protection with the Astra-mantra in all ten directions,
he should enter the sacrificial hall, which is filled with fire like the god Agni himself.
Facing either the east or the north, one should begin the specific ritual placement (*viśeṣanyāsa*).
Therein, first, with the Weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), which possesses a radiance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction... [k: ...endowed].
One should visualize the body, together with its exterior and interior, being consumed by fire from the tip of the big toe;
then, one should meditate upon that ash being scattered away by the wind of the armor-mantra (kavaca).
One should contemplate the Self as having the form of the Śiva-bindu;
then, one who is unconquered should unite the Power [Śakti] with it, thinking "I am He. (20)
Then, O Śāṅkarī, one should meditate upon the embodiment of knowledge with this mantra:
the Great Breath (H) mounted on the Staff (L), joined with the Navel (M).
Below that, the hip; then again, the left breast below;
and the throat and the left peak, adorned with the left mudrā. || 22 ||
O Goddess, this supreme *piṇḍa*, adorned with the *bindu*, the half-moon, space, *nāda*, *śakti*, and *bindu* again, is known as the "Ninefold" (*navātmaka*). 23.
This [mantra] is proclaimed as the bestower of all accomplishments along with its secret; it is devoid of the three syllables [at the beginning] and joined below with the six long vowels. (24)

One should assign the six limbs, beginning with the heart, according to the distinction of their seed-syllables; these are the syllables *kṣa*, *ya*, *ra*, *va*, *la*, and *ba*, which are radiant and adorned with the nasal bindu.
First, one should visualize the faces in sequence, beginning with the upward face;
then, for the sake of accomplishing the ritual of the individual limbs, one should assign [the mantras] to the forehead and other parts.
One should visualize the second [vowel] on the forehead and [the third] on the face;
having placed *i* and *ī* on the two eyes, one should assign *u* and *ū* to the two ears. (27)
Ṛ and Ṝ are in the nostrils; likewise, Ḷ and Ḹ are in the two cheeks.
E and Ai are in the lower and upper teeth respectively, and O and Au are in the two lips. (28)

One should assign the syllable *Aṃ* to the crest-lock with the Visarga; likewise, one should assign it to the tongue, the right shoulder, the staff-like arm, the hand, the fingers, and the nails. (29)
One should place the *ka*-group on the left in the same manner, starting from the beginning in sequence;
likewise, one should place the *ṭa* and *ta* groups, as before, on the hips, thighs, and so forth.
One should assign the 'ya' group [of letters] in sequence to the water for the feet (pādya), the two sides, the back, the belly, and the heart,
corresponding respectively to the skin, blood, flesh, and urine.
Having offered the five [elements]— flesh, bone, fat, semen, and breath— into the wells of the vital breaths, and then having assigned the limbs of the form, the wise one should invoke Śiva.
One should place the navel above the breath, and the right finger above that;
reaching as far as the left ear, this is Śiva, the bestower of all accomplishments.
For this is the supreme state of the great-souled Bhairava;
by means of this, the limbs [of the mantra] are to be formed as before, according to the differentiation of the vowels.
The Mūrtinyāsa, the Sṛṣṭinyāsa, the Tritattvanyāsa, and the eight [deities] together with their limbs, as well as Śiva along with his limbs—this is proclaimed as the sixteenfold Nyāsa. (35)
p.
44) Thereafter, perform the Śākta nyāsa upon this; listen as it is done:
having placed Parāparā upon the image, and Mālinī upon its faces. (36)
One should subsequently place the first three [syllables] on the crest, the heart, and the feet;
then [the remaining syllables] on the head, face, throat, heart, navel, genitals, thighs, and feet in sequence.
Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the eight Aghorīs and the limbs of the Vidyā as before,
one should then invoke the Śakti who is saluted by all yogins.
The individual soul (jīva), situated within the cavity of the vital breaths, possesses a brilliance equal to the fire of cosmic destruction;
it is exceedingly radiant, adorned on its left foot and marked upon its head with the bindu.
With his right knee joined [to the ground] and accompanied by the entire host of Mothers, he is worshipped;
when propitiated by this [rite], they all bestow the desired fruit. (40)
For this is proclaimed as the supreme state of the Mothers;
therefore, the practitioner who desires the highest accomplishment should recite this mantra. (41)
The immersion into the power of Rudra is eternally established here,
because this supreme power (parā-śakti) is proclaimed through this differentiation [as stated in Tantrāloka, verse 42].
Whatever accomplishments (siddhis) exist in the tantra, all of them are accomplished by her;
one should assign her limbs as before, according to the distinction of the vowels. (43)
The Form (mūrti) together with its faces, the Power (śakti), the triad of Vidyās,
the group of eight beginning with Aghorī, and likewise the five limbs of the Vidyā.
The supreme Śakti, together with her limbs, is declared to be the sixfold Nyāsa;
therefore, this Yāmala Nyāsa is for the attainment of all perfections.

This left-hand (vāma) ritual should be performed by those who rely on the path of liberation, or alternatively, it may be performed separately according to the distinctions of caste and mantras by those seeking its specific fruits. (46)
However many [deities] have been enumerated through their various divisions as designations for Śambhu, Śakti, and the individual soul (aṇu),
this fivefold ritual deposition (nyāsa) is considered to apply in exactly the same way to all of them.
However, whichever external [deity] is present in a particular location, that one is endowed with its own limbs;
thus, it is everywhere declared that this [mandala] consists of sixteen [deities].
Without contradicting one's own established practice, all sacrificial materials should be prepared according to the rules by the wise, through conceptualizations of existence and non-existence.
Then, taking the vessel for the *argha* offering— which is free from conceptualization regarding existence and non-existence—
one should purify it by burning it with the fire of the weapon-mantra and flooding it with the water of power.
If the purification of any other object here is to be performed,
it should be carried out by one who understands according to this very same method.
And one should not imagine even the slightest thing here that has not been purified. (Tattvasaṃgraha: "one should not imagine even the slightest thing").
Therefore, everything is indeed pure;
even that which is impure is pure.
Having filled it with that water and offered it with the six limbs,
one should consecrate all substances by making them nectar-like and purify them with it.
O you who are honored by the hosts of all yogis, I shall explain to you how one should perform the internal rite after having worshipped oneself. 54.
First, however, one should [visualize] the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) four finger-breadths below the navel;
this consists of a quartet: the earth, the ocean, the boat, and the bulb (kanda).
Each part of this trident's core (amalasaraka) should be one finger-breadth in width;
from that, one should fashion its shaft (daṇḍa), known as the "infinite" (ananta).
And here, from the limit of the uvula upwards, the knot is held to be above the *śūla*;
without piercing this, O Great Goddess, [one cannot cross] the great ocean of the net of bonds.
That person does not attain union with Śiva, nor the fourfold [perfections] of virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty. || 58 ||
The practitioner of mantra should contemplate the four limbs in the corners, starting from the southeast in due order;
he should likewise remember the four limbs in the directions, beginning with the east.
Above the *granthi* and below the trident, there must be a quadrangular platform (*catuṣkikā*).
They call that very thing the *vidyātattva*, conjoined with the three coverings (*chadana*). [In the manuscript *kh*, it reads "the two coverings."]
Between *ka* and *kha*, one should contemplate that very reality (*tattva*).
The reality of *ka* and *kha* is the Īśvara-tattva, which has the form of a lotus.
The wise one should contemplate [or: should then contemplate]. || 61 ||

Endowed with a pericarp and filaments, and possessing the seed-syllable, one should place the nine [syllables], beginning from the eastern petal and proceeding clockwise starting from the left, upon the blossoming white [lotus].
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and likewise Parā;
Kalavikaraṇī and Balavikaraṇī as well. || 63 ||
One should also place Balapramathanī and Sarvabhūtadamanī,
as well as Manonmanī, in the middle along the path of the sun.
One should also conceive another ninefold group starting from Vibhu in reverse order:
Vibhu, Jñānī, Kriyā, Icchā, Vāgīśī, and likewise Jvālinī. (65)
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī—all possess the radiance of the fire of time;
they are those who were previously established as the Śaktis of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara. || 66 ||
Those who reside in the center of the filaments of the petals are the lords of the mandalas;
one should contemplate them by means of the designations of sound, sun, moon, and fire. (67)
And the Lord Mahāpreta, laughing and conscious, with a body like ten million fires of cosmic destruction—thus is the entire seat [as described in the Parātriṃśikā]. || 68 ||
One should meditate on the three-pronged trident of power (śakti-śūla) rising from his navel,
emerging through the three voids and reaching as far as the limit of the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta).
Then, one should contemplate upon its peaks three lotuses belonging to Śakti;
white and presiding over all, this is the supreme seat (paramāsana).
Thereupon, one should contemplate above that the form known as Vidyā;
then, within that, the one called Ātman, together with the previously mentioned installation consisting of Śiva.

Then, in the center, one should visualize the supreme power (Parāśakti), and on the two sides, south and north, the power that is both supreme and non-supreme (Parāparā), who is red in color by her very nature and possesses great strength.
Having meditated upon her who assumes forms at will, who is somewhat fierce yet not terrifying, and another on the left horn who is terrifying and dark-brown; 73.

To the Goddess who assumes forms at will, who destroys the suffering of those who bow before her, the supreme Goddess who nourishes all, and whose radiance equals ten million times ten thousand moons; (74)
When the sixfold Śākta rite has been performed, one should contemplate [the deity] even in the forms (mūrti) and so forth;
thereafter, one should install the five limbs of the Vidyā in the directions beginning with the southeast (āgneyī).
One should likewise meditate, according to the prescribed rule, upon the limbs of Śakti and the limbs of Śiva in the south, in the proper sequence for Agni, Rākṣasa, and Vāyu.
However, one should meditate on the weapon-mantras in the directions starting with Indra (the east), and Locana in the center,
accompanied by the eight [mantras] beginning with Aghora and the eight [deities] beginning with Aghorī.

Having visualized all the guardians of the world (lokapālas) outside [the maṇḍala], together with their weapons, as being completely covered by [the protective circle] through their respective mantras, one should thereafter commence the recitation (japa).
Having become absorbed in their own nature, one should contemplate each [syllable] tenfold;
having meditated upon it as resembling a blazing fire, one should utter [the mantra] ending with *svāhā*.
The practitioner of mantra should perform [the oblation] either all at once or one by one for the successful accomplishment of the rite of homa;
thus has the mental sacrifice, which is collective in nature, been described. (80)
This is declared to be the trident, consisting of a single staff and possessing three powers.
O fair-faced one, without understanding this [nature of] the Śakti-trident in this way, [one does not truly know it]. (81)
Even after binding the khecarī-mudrā, one does not fly up from the surface of the earth;
this is declared to be the Śāmbhava [state], while that which ends with the eighth is considered Śākta.
One should know that the individual soul (āṇava) extends up to the fourth state; this is considered the triad of tridents.
According to the separate rules of sacrifice, one should meditate upon the wheel of power (śakticakra). || 83 ||
Having bound the *khecarī* [mudrā] by that means as well, he likewise abandons the surface of the earth.
Then, having consecrated the grains with the *mahāstra* [mantra] twenty-one times, (84)
One should cast [the oblations] in all directions, visualizing them like a blazing fire;
having meditated upon that house as being free from obstacles, one should withdraw [the visualization] and lead it toward the direction of the Lord (Īśa).
Then the wise man should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) with his five mouths:
namely, cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and likewise clarified butter.

One should consecrate the water of kuśa grass with the six-limbed mantra ending with the upward [gesture]; having bound the mudrās for the substances and nectar, one should contemplate its true nature (tattva). || 87 ||
With that [mixture], one should sprinkle the ground; with a small amount of the other, one should place it [elsewhere].
Then, one should perform the Vāstuyāga by means of the recitation of the Mālinī-mantra.
Having filled his joined palms with flowers while reciting the syllables beginning with *pha* (or *ha*, according to variant *k*),
and having meditated upon the path ending in *śakti*, he should cast it into the end of the syllable *na*.
Having offered perfumes, incense, and other offerings, one should worship Gaṇeśāna;
then, having placed the sixfold seat (ṣaḍuttham āsana) upon it with the Praṇava [Om], [one should proceed].
With the word "gām," one should worship Vighneśa with perfumes, incense, and so forth;
its limbs [are worshipped] by means of the letter *ga* joined with the six long vowels. (91)
Having meditated upon the elephant-faced one with three eyes, who has arisen in a dwarf form,
and having performed the ritual dismissal, one who desires success should worship the Great Weapon (Mahāstra). || 92 ||
Having bestowed infinite Dharma, as well as knowledge, detachment, and sovereignty,
one should place this seat consisting of six elements upon the pericarp;
having meditated upon [the deity] holding a sword and a shield, one should install him upon it.
Terrible, with great fangs, most fierce, and with a face knit in a frown. || 94 ||
Endowed with the six limbs of its own phonemes, surrounded by the Mothers of the Directions,
the six limbs are indeed composed of its own vowels, illuminated by the syllable *phaṭ*. || 95 ||
Having meditated upon that very form, one should then worship the eight Mothers;
one should simultaneously recollect Indrāṇī, holding a thunderbolt, on the eastern petal.

Then the wise one [should worship] the goddess of the southeast, holding a spear in her hand; then the goddess of the south, with a staff in her hand; and likewise the goddess of the southwest, the goddess of the west, and the goddess of the northwest. 97.
O Dear One, one should contemplate [the goddesses] simultaneously as being equipped with a sword, a noose, and a banner;
Kauverī with a mallet in her hand, and Īśānī joined with a trident. 98.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the independent tantra;
first, one should prepare a ritual jar consecrated more than a thousand times with mantras.
One should perform a thousand oblations there, and then, having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should dismiss [the deity]; thereafter, one should begin the sacrifice.
p.

52) Therein, first, having taken a jar made of gold or other [precious materials], free from flaws, and containing within it all mantras and medicinal herbs [the *Tantra* reads: "containing within it all jewels and medicinal herbs"],
Filled with fragrant water. || 101 ||
With a face like a mango sprout and a white garland-thread around his neck,
he was marked with the *rakṣoghna* tilaka and clothed in a pair of white garments. (102)

The water for the guest-offering (vārdhānī) should likewise be consecrated with one hundred and eight recitations of the root mantra and worshipped; however, it is specifically worshipped with a weapon-mantra (śastra).
Having offered the seat with scattered offerings (vikira), the wise one should thereafter worship Indra and the other deities in their respective directions using the prescribed mantras.
Then one should offer an uninterrupted stream from the *vārdhānī* vessel;
subsequently, one should circumambulate with the jar and speak this to the Lords of the World (*lokeśvara*).
O Śakra, by the command of Śiva, you must remain vigilant until the completion of the rite in your own quarter for the sake of pacifying obstacles. 106.
Having brought it there, one should first place the jar—which has become the embodiment [of the Supreme Goddess]—upon the seat;
to its southern side, one should set down the water-pot (vārdhānī). || 107 ||
Having placed [the deity], from the form of the self (ātma-mūrti) to the end of the objects of worship, into the water-pot (kumbha), the knower of mantras,
having worshipped [it] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, should worship this [deity] in the vessel for the guest-offering (vārdhānī).
Having prepared a fragrant mandala at the Brahma-position, the wise one should there worship the group of six or the group of three.
Or [it may be] in a triad, or even just one alone. || 109 ||
The scratching of the pit, the drawing of lines, the pounding, and the smearing;
likewise, the four-way path, the axle-enclosure, and the installation of the vajra.
One should perform the preparation of the *kuśa* grass matting, the enclosing sticks, and the seats with the Astra-mantra;
one should then install the Vidyā-mantra, thinking "I am Mohinī" (or "I am Aindrī").
Having assigned the syllables "Śiva" and "Oṃ" and having worshipped the pair again,
one should bring the sacrificial fire into a copper vessel or a clay bowl.
Having meditated upon it as the semen of Śiva, one should deposit it into the womb of the Vidyā;
