thereafter, one should offer five oblations with the very limbs of the Vidyā.
Then, all the rites beginning with *janana* are likewise completed; having thus performed them, thinking "it has been done," and recollecting the *Parāparā*, one should again offer the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Having fully honored the mother and the father of the fire, he should dismiss them;
then, having again lifted up the fire for the preparation of the sacrificial pap (caru) and other offerings.
Alternatively, having drawn out the fire of a blazing pyre by means of the left nostril and having confined it within the heart, one should then discharge it again through the right.
One should offer the full oblation as before; this is another procedure for the fire of Śiva.
Having beheld him in the form of Śiva, one should gradually effect the internal absorption of his self [into that]. (117)
The practitioner of mantra should perform the internal rite and then commence the fire sacrifice (homa),
having satisfied the root mantra with a hundred [recitations] and its six limbs according to the six-limbed ritual.
For the remaining classes of mantras, the libation (tarpaṇa) is performed with exactly one-tenth [of the number].
Then, he should cause the disciples—who are pure, bathed, and have fasted—to enter. 119.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the Gods of gods, who is present in the fourfold [forms] in sequence,
one should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the sacrificial porridge (caru), and likewise the tooth-stick.
The accomplishment of the sacrificial porridge (caru) is performed by the ritualists with milk and rice;
then, having performed the "falling together" (saṃpāta) rite with seven mantras, it is divided into six portions.
For Śiva, the fire, the guru, and the disciples, as well as for the two water-jars (vārdhānī and kumbha),
one should then provide a tooth-stick of equal length, produced from a milk-tree.
Its fall is auspicious if it goes toward the east, north, northeast, or upward; it is inauspicious elsewhere. Even in those [inauspicious] cases, there should be one hundred and eight oblations.
Then the preceptor should perform the external rite in all directions with this mantra:
"Oṃ kṣaḥ kṣaḥ, svāhā to all beings. (124)
Having sipped water for purification, performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), and worshipped Śaṅkara, he becomes pure. (125)
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) for the disciples and especially for himself,
he should perform his daily rites and so forth at dawn and then examine the dream.
One should proclaim what is auspicious to them; if there is inauspiciousness, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa).
Then, women well-adorned with fine garments and ornaments [should offer] flowers, fruits, and so forth.
Crossing over calamities, descending to auspicious regions, drinking intoxicants, decapitation, and the eating of raw meat. (128)
Beholding a deity face-to-face, as well as seeing excrement or being smeared with it— having seen such auspicious signs as these, one attains the desired perfection.

This very same thing, when occurring in a contrary manner, is proclaimed as a "bad dream" (*duḥsvapna*), such as eating cooked meat, anointing the body with oil, falling into a pit, and so forth. (130)

Having performed the expiation prescribed in the Tantras, the wise man should then effect his restoration to the status of the twice-born; thereafter, he should always perform worship of the gods, the sacred fire, the guru, and the Goddess.
One should not consume anything at all without first offering it to these [deities];
one should avoid the property of the gods, the property of the guru, and the property of Caṇḍī.
One who knows the mantra should not engage in fruitless activity even for a moment;
rather, he should be devoted to the practice of yoga or devoted to the practice of the mantra. (133)
Having caused [the disciples] to hear these and other such pledges, he should dismiss them;
thereafter, the bathing of the God of Gods, or of the disciples, or even of himself, [should take place]. (134)
One should perform [the rite] with the Śiva-pitcher, which removes all evil deeds;
thus has this ritual procedure (sāmaya-karma) been briefly proclaimed.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Observances (samaya), in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Now, when the Guru performs the initiation for these who abide by the rules (samaya), [he should proceed as follows].
Having performed that consecration (*adhivāsana*), [he should proceed]. || 1 ||
Then, he should properly stretch a cord toward the eastern direction;
from its center, he should mark the eastern and western points at equal intervals.
By means of a cord [stretched] from east to west, one should mark the north and south; likewise, from the western mark and also from the eastern mark, one should mark them in the same manner.
One should cast a long thread through the middle of the fish, extending from south to north;
then, measuring half the length of the intended field, one should mark the directions evenly from the center.
In the same way, from the corners of the square, one should drop threads in both clockwise and counter-clockwise directions upon those points for the sake of establishing the square.
In the case of this three-cubit [measure] based on the Vedas, one should first divide the eastern half of the cubit;
having set aside half a cubit on all sides, extending toward the east, north, and the intermediate directions.
One should divide the remainder of this into parts equal to the *guṇāṅgula* units,
with squares measuring three *aṅgulas* on the vertical and eightfold (twenty-four) on the horizontal.
Having set aside two parts each, [the lines] proceed again toward the south and north; likewise, from the fourth *jīva* line, they extend eastward from the sides of Brahmā.
Two pairs of crescent moons, each measuring half a part, should be placed;
between them, in the third [space], on the southern and northern sides.
The wise practitioner should form two half-moons within the *jīva* by means of internal rotation;
these two [lines] should reach the tips of the two half-moons, situated at the other vital point (*marman*) of those two.
One should create two pairs of half-moons for the outward-facing delusion;
likewise, one should fashion them within the Brahma-square, measuring one part and half a part respectively.
[Regarding the phrase "half a part"]:
Then, at the end of the second part, two lines should be drawn by the wise on both sides of the Brahmā-line, extending toward the east and measuring one-third of a part.
One should draw two lines situated at the upper tip of the single half-moon and joined to the end of the Brahma-thread, for the purpose of establishing the central prong. 13.
From the *jīva* at the front of those two sides, a thread is placed at an interval of one;
it should extend from the corner of the first and second half-moons to the opposite corner.
From the second life-force point of those same two, one should lead the thread from the corner of the first half-moon in the same manner as before, for the sake of accomplishing the pair of prongs.

And on the other half of the field, there is a boundary measuring two cubits and five *channas*; listen now as to how this is done. (Note: An alternative reading exists: *kṣetrārdhe cāpare daṇḍo dvikaracchannapañcakaḥ*, with the variant *kuryāddaṇḍamasya yathā śṛṇu*.)
Two parts [make] five; those five parts are concealed by the five seats. || 16 ||
The remaining other visible part, due to its breadth, should be measured in units;
it is six units wide and four units long, and below that is the amalasaraka (the base). || 17 ||
And its base below that should be four finger-breadths wide with a sharp point;
one should construct four doors in the cardinal directions of the primary field.
One should make it one cubit in length and half of that in width;
from the outside, one should make it double that size. Then, listen as to how the lotus is to be made.
One should draw circles according to the measure of each single part, like a Veda;
furthermore, there are sixteen life-lines (jīvasūtra), eight in each of the directions.
Furthermore, between each pair, one should drop as many [points] as that number;
among these, that which stands on the third circle is equal to the lateral life-line, [drawn] by rotation. || 21 ||
One should perform this up to this point, and thereafter bring forth the foremost of living beings;
wherever there is attachment, once that connection is firmly established.
Having done that there, the mantra-practitioner should lead [the lines] for the successful formation of the tips of the petals;
on each individual petal, he should fashion three filaments.
It should be made with sixteen finger-breadths (dviguṇāṣṭāṅgula),
and likewise, there should be three lotuses on the prongs.
Then the practitioner of mantra should worship with white powders and full offerings. || 24 ||
With red, black, yellow, and especially green [threads],
the pericarp should be made with the finest yellow [thread] according to the divisions of the base, middle, and tip.
The cluster of filaments should be made white, red, and yellow.
The petals are white in color, together with the protective rim. || 26 ||
Likewise, that yellow [square] is four-cornered; its outer part is equal to half the pericarp, and its sides are white, red, yellow, and black, starting from the southeast in due order.
The prongs are made with all four [colors], while the mandala is desired with three;
the staff should be blue and red, and the āmalasāraka is yellow.
One should cause the red-colored *śūla* to be fashioned as previously described;
subsequently, leaving a space of four finger-breadths to the east of the door.
The door may be triangular, square, circular, or variegated;
it may have one, two, or three chambers, being either symmetrical, ocean-like (sāmudra), or both.
It was beautifully adorned with many ornaments such as the splendor of its cheeks and neck;
it possessed various shapes and structures, and was provided with tiny houses made of creepers.
Thus, when this has been well accomplished here, one should perform the sweeping with a fragrant cloth and then carry out the ritual bath by means of the very same rite previously described.
Having entered as before, the practitioner of mantra should sit down as previously;
having performed all the previously mentioned installations of the fivefold nature of Bhairava.
One should place the Navātmaka Devadeva on the northern horn;
Bhairavasadbhāva in the center; and Ratiśekhara on the southern [horn].
He is adorned with the left ear by means of blood, skin, flesh, and urine.
One should designate that which is joined with the bindu and conjoined with the object of knowledge as Ratiśekhara. || 35 ||
Having performed the Śākta rite as before, the wise one should offer libations as previously described;
then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more with devotion, he should address him as follows: || 36 ||
O Supreme Lord, you alone have recognized me as your guru;
disciples impelled by the power of Śiva should be favored by you.
Therefore, since these various types have attained such states, you should bestow grace upon them by entering my body, so that I may become equal to you.
Having been told "I shall do so," with eyes blossoming from joy,
he should then contemplate the sixfold path presided over by this [deity].

One should contemplate that the five acts, beginning with creation, are to be accomplished by him; through his powers, he becomes the embodiment of the individual soul (jīvamūrti), which is twofold: both supreme (parā) and non-supreme (aparā).
Through the distinction between the formed and the formless, this [power] attends upon me as well;
those mantras, such as the *hṛdaya* and others, become its instruments. (41)
Having meditated upon Śiva as being thus, with an inner self absorbed in Him,
one should contemplate oneself as identical with Him and revolve Śiva tenfold.
Having recited all the mantras situated within the inner enclosure three times,
he should then bind the white turban, which has been consecrated seven times with the ninefold self-mantra.
Then one should perform the Śivahasta rite, which effects the loosening of bonds;
having washed the hand with scented water by means of another hand.
Smeared with fragrance, one should worship the deity together with his limbs (the retinue), though omitting the seat;
likewise, one should perform the touching, the grasping, and the union within oneself.
And [he experiences] separation from that, its extraction, the cutting of bonds, and so forth; thus, having attained the state of a pati (Lord), he pervades the phenomenal world as Śiva. (46)
Then, one should meditate upon oneself as distinct [from the deity], yet possessing qualities equal to those [of the deity]:
"I myself am this one situated in the mandala, like a witness over all actions. (47)
I abide in the fire as the locus for the oblation; I am established in the ritual jar until the conclusion of the sacrifice for the pacification of obstacles. (48)
And in order to accomplish the severance of the bonds within the body of the disciple,
I, residing directly within my own body, am the agent of the act of grace.
Having reflected upon all this, the mantra-practitioner should contemplate the path to be purified—that path by which he intends to perform the initiation for his disciples. (50)
Right there he should contemplate everything and proceed to the state free from affliction;
having become non-different from that, he should then reflect upon this: || 51 ||
I alone am the supreme reality; this entire world is within me.
I abide as the presiding ground and the agent of everything.
A living being who has attained equality with that is said to be liberated;
having reflected thus, one should once again take recourse to the primordial [reality] that is to be purified. (53)
There, one should visualize one of the fires of the disciple-maṇḍala as being present;
having projected the path to be purified upon the bodies of the disciples as previously described. (54)
One should take recourse in the meditation on one's own pervasion by means of each respective mantra,
having first bound the cage of fetters— whether adventitious, innate, or pertaining to Śakti.
Having encircled the three points— the two arms, the neck, and the tip of the crest—
with the thread of the triple-guṇas while reciting one's own mantra, one should then invoke the reality (*tattva*) and worship it.
And having fully satisfied [them], || 56 ||
Then, the wise one should lead that pervasive womb of the wombs to be purified into the path ending in Māyā; indeed, he should lead that same pure Vidyā [into it]. (57)
Having performed the satiation (saṃtarpaṇa) in that [fire], the wise one should strike the disciple with the weapon-mantra (astra),
and then again touch him on the heart with the hand of Śiva.
One should perform its grasping by not being separated from even a single ray;
having gone through the path of the channels (nāḍī), it is encapsulated by the *haṃsa-hṛt* mantra.
Then, having established [the deity] within himself, the mantra-practitioner should contemplate the impregnation (garbhādhāna) in the womb,
endowed with all the rites of gestation by means of the three-syllable half-verse mantra.

O Sulocanā, the wise practitioner of mantra should effect the birth [of the deity] through the accomplishment of the capacity for the state of being the enjoyed and the enjoyer, by means of [the mudrā] located on the tip of Dakṣa’s horn.
The wise practitioner should duly offer fifteen oblations with the *astra* and other mantras, preceded by the *pibanī* mantra, and also with the supreme (*parā*) mantra.
Then, the wise should perform for him the severing of the bonds by means of another [mantra],
after having addressed either Bhuvaneśa or Tattveśvara.
p.
65) [Regarding] the portions of enjoyment... after that, one should command this:
"O Lord of the World, by the command of Śiva, you must not [obstruct] this practitioner. || 64 ||
An obstruction should be created for the traveler’s path to safety;
then, one should perform the upward-throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*) with that same [mantra] consisting of six and a half syllables.
For the sake of purifying the individual paths, one should offer three oblations each, meditating separately, due to the connection with mantras that have not been fully pervaded.
Then one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the supreme mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ";
having raised the child, one should cause him to abide within oneself and within his own body.
Having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the wise one should offer three oblations with the Mahāpāśupata-weapon mantra for the sake of purifying the reversed order and so forth.
O Supreme Goddess, having dismissed Vāgīśī, one should then contemplate that pure reality as dissolved within the impure. (69)
When the purification through the pervasion of the subsequent time has thus been performed with diligence,
one should sever that noose of the arms and offer it into the fire together with clarified butter.
When the principle of Māyā has been purified, as well as the bond at the throat,
the wise one [should perform] the rite of initiation in its entirety for the complete purification of the path ending with Māyā.
In ritual actions where no mantra has been specified, the wise one should employ the Aparā;
and likewise, from the beginning of the Vidyā up to the end of the Sakala, he should employ the Parāparā.
One should join the eightfold sequence beginning with *pibanī* above the level of Īśvara.
Nor, O wise one, should one visualize the group of six limbs above the entire [body]. || 73 ||
Whatever rite is enjoined by the ritual rules should be performed in the Niṣkala [state] by means of the Parā [mantra];
however, in the Viśuddha [cakra], at the end of the Sakala [state], the wise one should cut the top-knot (śikhā).
Having offered the clarified butter, he should then bathe the disciple in due order;
having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and worshipped the Lord of Gods, he should fill the sacrificial ladle (sruva) with ghee.
Having thus established the disciple within himself, he should recollect the root mantra;
likewise, he should contemplate Śiva, Śakti, himself, the disciple, the clarified butter, and the fire.
Unifying [the breath], one should gradually proceed to the dvādaśānta with undistracted mind;
having established the kumbhaka there, one should meditate upon the Lord who is both with and without parts.
One should remain undisturbed until the consumption of the clarified butter is complete;
thus joined with the supreme reality by the Guru, who is the very form of Śiva. (78)
One whose bond of illusion (māyā) has been burnt no longer returns to the state of a bound soul (paśu);
this is declared to be the rule regarding the rite of initiation (dīkṣā) in the earthly realm (bhuvana).
(67) Having set aside the rules for the other paths as well as the rules for Śiva-yoga,
and having abandoned the reverse-order ritual, one proceeds with double the effort on the path of the *tattvas*.

And likewise, on the path of the phonemes (varṇa-mārga) it is fourfold; on the path of the words (pada-vartman) it is eightfold; on the path of the mantras (mantra-mārga) it is also eightfold; and on that which is called the path of the parts (kalā), it is likewise twofold.
In the *Trikhaṇḍa*, that very same [purification] is proclaimed as having twenty qualities;
thus, the purification of all paths has been briefly described.
"Now listen as the ritual duties of the practitioner and the teacher are being described.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, the Chapter on Ritual Initiation (*kriyādīkṣā*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
Now begins the tenth chapter:
Furthermore, [one should worship] one who is endowed with the auspicious marks and is intent upon the means of attaining supernatural powers.
One who knows the scriptures, self-controlled, wise, free from greed, honest, and steadfast. || 1 ||
Likewise, without having examined him, the Guru should employ him in the role of an accomplisher (sādhaka),
after having worshipped the Supreme Lord according to the prescribed rite as before.
In the second [case], as before, there is a vessel made of gold or other materials, free from blemishes;
in all instances, it rests upon the southern petal of the central lotus.
One should worship the individual mantras of the leaders with flowers and other offerings;
having gratified him with a thousand [offerings], one should perform the consecration.
Having placed [the image] upon an auspicious, noble throne made of Śrīparṇa wood, facing either eastward or northward, bathed, and adorned with flowers and other ornaments; || 5 ||

Having properly assumed the body of the mantra and having duly performed the auspicious rites, amidst the resounding blasts of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, and the auspicious chanting of the Vedas; || 6 ||
Having performed his consecration with all royal honors,
and having meditated upon him as equal to Sadāśiva, one should then adorn him as well.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods once more, the wise one should impart the mantra to him;
accompanied by flowers, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds, he should place the water-vessel containing the Lord.
He too, likewise assuming that form upon his head, having consecrated the southern [form],
should then manifest the power of Rudra by means of the Astra-mantra.
Embraced by her, he should satisfy her mantra with a thousand [offerings];
from that time forward, being devoted to her, he shall become equal to her in qualities.
This is the consecration of the preceptor; it is performed without the ritual procedure of mantras, but rather accompanied by the stage of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
Thus, this state is to be attained, yet it is difficult for those of unrefined self to reach;
therefore, the practitioner, for the sake of attaining success in mantra, should observe the mantra-vow.

Having performed this and bathed as prescribed for the consecration, one should recite the mantra of the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyādhipa*) one hundred thousand times; one should then perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for him with a tenth part of that amount.

Having performed the consecration as before, one should mutter the Brahmaśiras mantra; becoming focused on that and absorbed in it, one should do so for two hundred thousand recitations without weariness.
O Goddess, one should recite two hundred thousand times the Rudrāṇī, four times the Puruṣṭuta,
and five hundred thousand times the Mahāpāśupata.
Adorned with white, red, yellow, black, and variegated garments and ornaments, one who is thus protected by these mantras shall become peerless. (16)
Invulnerable to all malevolent beings and empowered by the splendor of the mantra,
having thus observed his vows, he may accomplish whatever he desires.
Having offered the *argha* to him, one should reverently recite the nine-syllable mantra one hundred thousand times;
and following the fire-oblation (*homa*) with superior substances, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with a tenth part of that amount. (18)
Those who know the tradition say that the *mahākṣmāpāla* coins are the best and so forth;
having doubled [the number] for the middling ones, one should likewise triple it for the inferior ones. (19)
Clarified butter, guggulu resin, and human fat are considered equal to mahāmāṃsa; curd, bilva fruit, milk, and lotus are proclaimed to be equal to earth.
The dhātrī, dūrvā, amṛtā, and fish are considered to be equal to clarified butter.
Then, one should perform [the rites] with sesame seeds and other materials in the sequence of nine, six, and three times [the amount].
Having first performed this preliminary service in this manner, the wise one should offer the argha for the sake of accomplishment.
Having offered the argha, he should recite the mantra until the desired accomplishment is attained.

O Goddess, by one hundred thousand [recitations], the lord of the earth, together with his servants, army, and vehicles, is brought under control; by two hundred thousand, one shall obtain a kingdom. (23)
Through three [perfections] there is the attainment of treasures; through four, the attainment of powers;
through five, the entire earth; and through six, the host of apsarases. (24)
With seven [repetitions], one attains the seven worlds; with ten, one becomes equal to him [the deity].
From there, O Maheśvarī, by means of fifty, one goes to the end of the unmanifest (avyakta).

Success is achieved for one who has performed ten million recitations (*koṭi-japta*): up to the level of *māyā* by sixty hundred-thousand, up to the level of *īśvara* by eighty hundred-thousand, and up to the limit of the earth along with all its parts. (26)
Alternatively, having performed the service as described, one who possesses a heroic mind should carry out this ritual on the night of a Kṛṣṇa-Bhūta day.
Having performed the previously mentioned sacrifice and offered the subsequent substances, the mantra-practitioner,
with his body erect and remaining perfectly motionless, should recite the mantra while facing north.
Meanwhile, the mistresses of yoga arrived from all sides,
raising a most terrible and extremely dreadful clamor.
Having fallen to the ground, they remain there, encircling the Lord of Sādhakas within;
having paid homage to them, he pierces his own left side.
By offering the *argha* to them with that [mantra] thus produced, one becomes equal to them;
and the preceptor (*ācārya*) as well, observing silence, should perform this daily for six months.
As for the fifteen mantras which were previously mentioned by me to you—
Bound by the previous ritual placement (nyāsa), he performs the fire-ritual three times a day.
Having performed the sacrifice previously described, which is encircled by the three powers, one who has taken recourse to celibacy should meditate upon the trident mentioned before.
Then the teacher should consecrate himself at the beginning and at the end;
thus, having fulfilled his vow, the practitioner becomes the best among those who know the mantras. (34)
Performing the activity of restraint and grace, one is not obstructed.
One should place the three [syllables] of the root-mantra in the triad of the beginning, middle, and end of the two pure [mantras]. 35.
One should place the Eye on the palm of the left thumb and the Weapon on the forefinger;
then, with the portion beginning "akṣahrīṃ" (or "namo hrīṃ"), one should install the Assembly of Sounds.
By means of this [mantra] "Naphahrīm," the wise one [should worship] the form of Śakti,
as well as the root [mantra], through the practice of the inverted Mahāmudrā.
"The placement of the limbs in their respective locations is known as the general nyāsa.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on Consecration, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra.
Now begins the eleventh chapter:
Hereafter, I shall fully explain initiation, which is exceedingly difficult to attain.
which brings about both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and which produces immediate conviction. || 1 ||
In this [practice], nothing such as a mandala or a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) is required;
nor is there any prior requirement for ritual placement (nyāsa), bathing, and so forth, according to one's preference.
Having entered the sacrificial hall, which is well-smeared and beautifully adorned,
he, wearing fine garments and ornaments and decorated with excellent flowers, should face either the east or the north.
Recalling the blazing spear, one should contemplate the body as completely consumed by fire, from the tips of the feet up to the crown of the head, through the application of the Mahāmudrā.

And for the sake of accomplishing the body, one whose mind is absorbed in that meditation should contemplate Mālinī, who possesses the luster of nectar, through the practice of the direct order (anuloma).
Then one should contemplate the path to be purified within the body as previously described;
having thus purified the constituent elements, one should lead them to the state of immortality by means of Śakti alone.
O Dear One, the knower of the ritual procedure should employ Mālinī situated in the middle of the *parā-sampuṭa* for all rites, or else he may employ *Parā* alone.
Having first worshipped Gaṇeśa for the pacification of obstacles,
one should then worship the lineage of gurus, beginning with one's own guru.
Below Gaṇeśa, one should worship the entire collection of mantras; thereafter,
one should perform the full worship right there for half [the number] of their lords.
One should worship the Vidyā at the bottom of the last [column], and likewise the Maheśvarī Vidyā;
one should place the Kula-Śakti within the group of Mantra-Vidyās.
In the east, south, west, and north are the four goddesses beginning with Māheśī;
likewise, starting with Indrāṇī, they are situated at the ends of the petals beginning from the northeast.
There, one should place the deity above with this seed-syllable (bīja) in the form of a peak (kūṭa),
the individual soul (jīva) situated upon the trident and pervaded by the staff (daṇḍa).
Then [he places them] below the right fingers, then on the left breast,
then on the navel and the throat, and finally as ornaments on the left shoulder.
Subsequently joined with the tongue of Śiva, and above that with the upper lip, he is declared to be the sovereign of all the circles of Yoginīs. || 14 ||
From the mere utterance of this [mantra], the consciousness proclaimed by others shall arise;
thereafter, one should worship the group of eight heroes according to the procedure taught for Śakti.
Having worshipped with abundant and various offerings such as perfumes, incense, garlands, and so forth, one should assign a name preceded by the syllable "Śrī" and ending with the word "pāda. (16)
Then, having summoned a disciple who has been thoroughly tested in many ways and having sprinkled him with the power of Rudra (rudra-śakti), he should place him before the deity.
Having gazed upon his two arms, one should inflame them with the power of Rudra;
likewise, one should place a flower upon the two hands smeared with fragrance. (18)
Having meditated on those two as being without support, one should contemplate them as drawn in by the power (śakti);
then, having bound their eyes as before with the eye-mantra consecrated by power (śakti).
Then she should cast the flower; that power resides in her hand.
Wherever that flower falls, one should recognize that as her *kula*.
Having opened his mouth, he should then cast him down upon his feet;
then, the knower of yoga, having worshipped the wheel on his head and in his two hands, [should proceed].
One should direct those two hands with all one's power until they reach the crown of the head;
this is declared to be the rite of the Śiva-hand, which produces immediate conviction.
Thereafter, one should cause caru made from fruits such as dates to be offered;
having assumed a body supported by Śakti, one should place it before the child.
Drawing back the right hand by means of the practice of scattering flowers, the mantra-practitioner,
with his mind absorbed in that meditation, should cause [the disciple] to take the sacrificial oblation (caru).
Having raised it by means of the application of Śiva’s hand, one should lead it to the mouth;
by this very procedure, [one should take] that which has arisen from a milk-tree.
O Goddess, one should give a tooth-stick sixteen finger-breadths in length.
By observing the movement of these, the mantra-practitioner should examine the descent of power (śaktipāta). (26)
"By means of the distinctions of weak, intense, and so forth, [the wise one] [attains] the weak, intense, and so forth;
thus is this initiate (samayin) described as established according to the path that has been taught. (27)
And when the yogin, with his mind dedicated to him alone, desires to undergo initiation,
he should worship that Kuleśa in due order, as before.
Having worshipped him as before, the wise teacher should gaze upon the disciple’s straight body,
contemplating the *śakti* extending from the tips of his feet to the crown of his head.
Then, one should project the path to be purified, which consists in the state of pervading all paths,
according to the previously mentioned method through the divisions of the *śakti-tattva* and so forth.
Then, having sat down, one should perform this ritual procedure for him:
beginning from the root-purification, [one should visualize] the Śakti, possessing the luster of a blazing fire.
One whose mind has attained the contemplation of the object to be purified and its purification should apply [the fire];
thus she burns all things to be purified, becoming free from disease. (32)
The yogi should contemplate [the soul] merged within Śiva, whether in his partless (niṣkala) or his manifest (sakala) form;
once joined to the path, it brings nourishment to its own kind.
It performs [the purification] and burns away other heterogeneous groups;
by means of this, the one of great intelligence purifies this disciple. (34)
One should attentively observe the collection of signs beginning with bliss;
bliss, rising, trembling, sleep, and the fifth is reeling. (35)
Thus, by means of this power of penetration, according to its degrees of mildness, intensity, and so forth,
one may perform the paralyzing of fetters (pāśastobha) and the seizing of the bound soul (paśugrāha) at will.
Furthermore, one should perform the ritual application (niyoga) of what has been grasped for the sake of consuming the remainder;
or else, this [experience of] possession does not arise for anyone at all.
Therefore, one should burn this [body] simultaneously with power, both internally and externally.
Being thus consumed by that [power], it is like a tree whose roots have been severed. || 38 ||
He casts reproach upon the back of the Kāśyapī earth;
yet one should not abandon even such a person as this. || 39 ||
For one who possesses the necessary fitness for initiation into the ritual of the separate principles (pṛthaktattva),
he should cause it to be performed according to the procedure for the practice of the principles that will be described hereafter.
Thus, for this seeker of liberation who has been duly initiated, the remaining conduct—
consisting of the Kulakrameṣṭi accompanied by the five states— is to be prescribed.
One who is hungry, however, should perform the ritual consecration of yoga correctly;
having worshipped the body there as before with extensive and wise deities. (42)
Having awakened Śiva by means of eight lamps made of gold and other materials with red wicks and ghee, one should worship Him using a conch shell along with the eight Kulas.
In a vessel containing all kinds of jewels and medicinal herbs, filled with fragrant water,
he should consecrate him by means of that [water] according to the procedure prescribed for the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta).
This is the consecration of the Ācārya, endowed with the station of authority;
he should likewise offer sixty-four lamps made of *piṇḍas* and other materials.
Indeed, in the very rite of consecration, both [the disciple and the master] are known by the entire assembly of yogis; therein, the guru shall be the bestower of liberation.
To these two, the yogi should impart all three kinds of knowledge;
he should then give his own command regarding the performance of his own practice.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Section on Initiation, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. || 11 ||
Now begins the twelfth chapter:
Then, having heard these exceedingly clear words of the God of Gods, [he spoke].
With eyes wide open in great joy, she brings delight to the entire world.
Satiated by the nectar of contentment, the Goddess, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods, bowed to the slayer of Andhaka and spoke these words once more: || 2 ||
"You previously stated that a yogi should practice yoga;
O Destroyer of Tripura, please tell me how that practice is to be performed."
Thus addressed by the Mother of the World, Bhairava, the destroyer of fear,
spoke these words, both gracious and profound, he of noble intellect.
O Goddess, listen to the method for the practice of yoga as it is being told by me,
by means of which a yogi, having become steady here, shall attain perfection.
In a cave, or even in an underground chamber— silent, very beautiful,
and entirely free from all disturbances— a yogi should practice yoga.
He has conquered his posture, conquered his mind, conquered his vital breaths, and conquered his senses;
he has conquered Māra, conquered anger, conquered agitation, and is free from distress.

Either by means of the differentiation of objects, or else through the differentiation of the mind, the Lord of Yogins should accomplish everything from the earth up to the power (śakti). [Kh: Having released it, he should compose himself. 8

The sixfold division of the target (lakṣya) is traditionally taught as it truly is, according to the distinctions of space, form, the point (bindu), phoneme (varṇa), world (bhuvana), and sound (dhvani).
The void (vyoma) is proclaimed to be threefold— by way of the distinction between external and internal, and by their combination— and the point (bindu) is held to be tenfold.
Shaped like a kadamba flower bud and resembling a shimmering star,
though it is one, it is considered tenfold through its various distinctions such as white and so forth.
Sound is tenfold due to its divisions such as Ciñciṇī and Cīravāka;
and although the body is divided into two types according to the distinction between the self and the atoms, it is manifold.
There is no limit to the number of worlds; that [number] consists of fifty [crores]. Even when a single goal is accomplished, indeed, a hundred thousand [others] follow as a consequence here.
When there are various other fruits, that is called "piercing the target" (lakṣyabheda);
where there is only a single fruit, that is considered "differentiation of mind" (cittabheda). || 14 ||
One whose self is purified by the initiation of the fire-oblation (homadīkṣā) and who possesses the instruction on immersion (samāveśa)—
such a person should practice yoga at the very outset when desiring to accomplish it. (15)

Having placed the supreme seed-syllable (*parābīja*) upon the two hands, the wise one should contemplate the Śakti by means of the application of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) in the inverted rite. (16)
Then, resembling a blazing fire from the tips of his feet to the top of his head,
he performed prostration and thereafter held his breath, fixing it in his heart.
One should meditate upon the supreme seed-syllable in its own form as intensely radiant;
one should contemplate its three measures as having emerged from the three voids.
Then, after a hundred tālas, the yogin shall attain absorption;
for even a slayer of a Brahmin will [attain it] within seven days if he practices every day. (19)
One whose body has been thus possessed should perform the ritual procedure as it has been described;
however, this applies to one for whom the sequence of the rite of possession has already been performed by the Guru at the outset.
Having paid homage to Gaṇeśa and recollected the lineage of the three Gurus, he should begin the conquest of the stages through the power of his latent impressions (vāsanā). || 21 ||
With one-pointed mind, one should meditate thus: "May my body be perfectly possessed [by the deity]," visualizing one's own body as resembling gold, four-cornered, and marked with a vajra. (22)
Thereafter, heaviness sets in after twenty-seven days;
from the seventh day onwards, a state of stupor arises in him.
Within six months, one shall conquer disease and become like molten gold;
within three years, one shall possess a vajra-body and the prowess of nine nāgas. (24)
O Goddess, this pure *dhāraṇā* pertaining to the earth has been proclaimed to you; it is the first [state] within the previously mentioned fifteenfold division. (25)
One should meditate upon the body as active, with a luster like molten gold, seated within a square mandala adorned with vajras. (26)
Within seven days it attains weightiness; after a month, one is freed from disease;
and within six months, one knows everything existing beneath the earth according to its true nature.
In three years, he enjoys the earth girt by the seven oceans.
This is declared the second division; now hear the third.
In that very same way, one should meditate upon the body as being devoid of activity;
one obtains the previously mentioned fruit, including that which pertains to Pātāla.
In the fourth [stage], one should meditate on [the deity] located in the heart, twelve finger-breadths in length,
in the form of the original syllable, extending from the right to the left, without weariness.
Having attained everything previously described, one becomes the lord of Pātāla;
indeed, that very state becomes stable when the fifth [element] is rendered inactive.
The wise practitioner should likewise meditate on the sixth [center] as yellow, resembling a shimmering sun, and the seventh as black, dense, and waveless.
When both of these have become firm, one knows and enjoys the three worlds—Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar—in the very years previously mentioned. || 33 ||
One should contemplate the entire Self, possessing the luster of gold, situated within the heart, with its own radiance illuminating the interior of the whole body. (34)
When this ninth [state] has become stable, the wise one knows and enjoys the seven worlds—distinguished by their activity and other attributes—as before. || 35 ||
One should meditate upon two [forms], yellow and resembling the orb of the sun, as before;
by the very path previously described, one attains the world of Brahmā. (36)
One should meditate upon [the deity] as yellow, shining below, possessing two forms, and great as before; having become equal to me, one goes to my world. || 37 ||
One should contemplate the all-illuminating yellow radiance, both external and internal;
one shall thereby attain the sovereignty over the hundred Rudras.
Thus, having practiced the earth-principle (pṛthivītattva) in fifteen ways, yogis do so for the sake of attaining yoga, out of a desire for its fruits. (39)
At the time of initiation, the wise should employ a person in that very area where his latent impression has arisen by the power of his own aptitude. (40)
Whoever is joined to a particular reality does not turn back from it;
having attained all its fruits and being united with Śiva, he is liberated.
Even one who is not yet disciplined, having attained the state of a Lord of the Worlds through the higher purification,
reaches the state of Śiva once the bonds of saṃsāra have been burnt away.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, on the first dhāraṇā, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. || 12 ||
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain this Vāruṇī Dhāraṇā.
By means of which, through perfected yoga, one becomes the lord of the depths of the waters. || 1 ||
The yogi should meditate on the body as being situated within water—[the reading "consisting of water" (jalātmakam) is authenticated by the *Svacchanda-tantra*]—as white, cool, and very tranquil;
he should contemplate it both internally and externally, thinking that nothing else exists. || 2 ||
For one who practices in this manner, moistness shall arise after seven days;
he will certainly be freed from diseases of bile within a month. (3)
With supple limbs and a gentle gaze, and with dark, curly hair,
the lord of yogis becomes one who rains like a cloud after three years.
Thus has been described this first pure concentration (śuddha-dhāraṇā) pertaining to Varuṇa;
now I shall further explain it as divided by its various distinctions.
O Goddess, one should contemplate one's own body as before— active, white, and situated upon water— with the inner self absorbed therein.
Within seven days, one is freed from all diseases arising from bile (pitta);
within six months, stability is attained if one has become absorbed in that [practice].
The consciousness of the water-sheath arises from these three [elements];
though it is devoid of activity and differentiation, it is everywhere comparable to Varuṇa. (8)
He goes to the principle of Varuṇa; he should practice the stages (bhūmikās) in succession.
As before, one should [visualize] the Self situated in the middle of the throat, twelve finger-breadths [above it].
Constantly remembering the Lord of the Essence of Water, one will certainly behold Him before long;
once He is seen, the vision becomes steady when the fifth [element], the Self, is stabilized in its own nature.
Even when the lunar orb has become stable in its two-fold division and is densely enveloped, it attains a state of equality with that [light]; from that, she who possesses a complete form [arises].
One should contemplate, filling the body with white-colored radiance;
that very [body] attains stability once it has reached a state of perfect steadiness therein.
Then, one should contemplate that which has the appearance of the moon's orb released from the clouds;
thereby one attains the state of being its lord, and the second [stage] reaches stability. (13)
Therefore, one should contemplate that light as the illuminating white [element];
from that, one attains the state of a Vidyeśvara arising from the veil of water.
When one meditates on the white radiance pervading one's own body, and when that [radiance] is well-stabilized, one attains stable sovereignty over all things situated therein. || 15 ||
When stability in the three states has been achieved, there arises an identity with the reality to be meditated upon;
and in the second [state], there arises the form of consciousness as its Lord.
In the second [case], elsewhere he becomes a steady knower of yoga equal to that;
in the sixth, he attains lordship over all, but in the second, elsewhere there is downfall.
(86) Thus,
this procedure, which bestows the accomplishment of the fivefold fruit, should be known by those who know the ritual rules within the fifteenfold division among all the principles (tattvas). 18.
Whatever other fruit than this has been mentioned, and whatever else will be spoken of, all that should be understood as an incidental result arising from a lack of critical inquiry. (19)
Thus has Vāruṇī been described with its fifteen divisions;
now hear about Āgneyī for the sake of the yogis' accomplishment of yoga.
One should contemplate the body as a triangle enveloped by garlands of red flames;
O Goddess, within seven days, its sharpness arises.
The practitioner is freed from all ailments arising from wind and phlegm within a month;
he becomes free from excessive sleep, eats much, and has scanty excrement and urine. (22)
By his will, he burns away other manifest objects at the end of the seasons;
having become equal to fire after three years, he sports like fire according to his desire.
When enraged, he burns everything, including the mountains, forests, and groves;
one should contemplate oneself as mounted upon a triangular mandala. (24)
The wise one, by means of the distinctions such as activity and so forth, shall be freed from diseases within seven days; after six months, he becomes like fire.
In three years, he perceives the complete principle of fire (tejas-tattva).
Whatever is seen in one differentiation of its power becomes stabilized in each of its various differentiations.
As before, meditating on himself as being situated in the middle of the palate with the radiance of a blazing fire, he perceives all the lords of the principles (*tattva*) in succession. (27)
Meditating upon that which resembles fire enveloped in smoke and has the appearance of the solar disc,
one attains equality with the Lord of the Principle of Fire (tejas-tattva) from within it.

One should meditate upon that entire [deity] right there— whose mass of darkness is destroyed by its radiance and whose splendor is like a smokeless fire— and one shall attain the state of being its lord.
There, one should contemplate that radiance which has the appearance of the light of the midday sun;
when it has become perfectly stable therein, one attains the state of being a Lord of Mantras.
There, one should manifest a splendor resembling a jewel-lamp;
having attained identity with that, the yogi reaches the state of being the Lord of the Lords of Mantras. || 31 ||
Meditating on that light which pervades everything, both external and internal,
he does not fall from that state until the time of universal dissolution, remaining unbroken.
But at the time of withdrawal, he attains the supreme, peaceful state of Śiva.
Thus has this fifteenfold concentration on fire (vahnidhāraṇā) been described. (33)
Relying upon the wind-element concentration (vāyavī dhāraṇā), one should contemplate one's own body as black, circular, marked with six dots, moving, and making the sound "cu-cū."
Through the cessation of diseases born of phlegm, one becomes mobile like the wind;
the yogi should practice this for six months with his inner self absorbed therein.
Having traveled a hundred yojanas, he returns in a single moment without fatigue.
After three years, he shall truly assume the form of Vāyu.
He pulverizes masses of mountains,
uproots even trees,
and when enraged, he brings down Śakra.
Together with his servants, forces, and vehicles. || 37 ||
One should contemplate one's own body as resembling blue collyrium;
one obtains everything previously mentioned within six months—of this there is no doubt. (38)
Having attained identity with it, one perceives the element of air after three years;
one should meditate on one's own form, resembling collyrium, between the eyebrows.
He beholds all the swift-moving lords of the wind-element as having the luster of sapphire veiled by clouds and the form of the solar disc.
Meditating upon it, one attains equality with it when one becomes fully absorbed in it;
at that time, one should contemplate everything there as resembling a split sapphire.
He attains the status of that mantra-lord, and thereafter even lordship over it;
when that all-pervading syllable is meditated upon as radiant energy, he shall attain [that state]. || 42 ||
Then, one attains invincibility therein as [the breath] spreads upwards and downwards;
thus has been described the divine concentration (dhāraṇā) arising from the vital air. 43.
Having meditated upon one's own body as being like the wind and recollecting its absence, the yogi attains emptiness within seven days. (44)
Within a single month, even if bitten by the lords of serpents, one does not faint;
freed from all diseases, one is rid of wrinkles and grey hair. (45)

Within six months, he will take on the form of the sky and pass even through subtle apertures; after three and a half years, he will become like the void itself— as is established in the *Svacchandatantra*.
By his mere will he becomes a massive body, and likewise by his will a subtle body;
he is neither cuttable nor pierceable, yet he perceives the earth as full of holes.
By contemplating one's own body as being like the interior of a crucible filled with the residue of the sap of a hundred flowers, the knowledge of space arises after three years.
One shall obtain all the previously mentioned fruits within seven days or other such periods;
likewise, one should contemplate that [form] on the forehead, extending twelve finger-breadths in length.
He beholds all those respective lords of the principles (tattveśas) standing before him in succession;
by meditating on them as having the appearance of the lunar orb eclipsed by Rāhu, he attains identity with them.
One should meditate upon that which is situated there, entirely resembling the orb of the moon;
thereby one attains the state of the Lord of Mantras, and through its radiance, even the nature of the moon.

By means of that very [power] which flows downward, the wise one, having attained the state of Mantreśvara and Īśatva, both externally and internally, shall obtain incomparable higher knowledge (vijñāna). || 52 ||
And by that [power] which spreads upwards, having the nature of nectar like moonlight,
one attains absolute independence and is no longer obstructed anywhere.
Thus, the retention (dhāraṇā) of the five principles has been fully described.
Pure consciousness abiding in the pure path constitutes the fivefold possession by the elements (bhūtāveśa) here. (54)
Fixing his mind upon those very [perceptions], he effects the destruction of his own despondency;
for even in another cognition, he may do so by his own will.
One should properly stabilize the mind; through that, one enjoys its fruit.
Even though this [meditation] is but one, it is differentiated by its internal subdivisions. (56)
It becomes an obstacle therein; one should not establish a fixed residence there.
Those who do establish a fixed residence there will not attain the supreme fruit.

When the fivefold dhāraṇās are mastered, the eight qualities of the Piśācas are attained; alternatively, for yogins, the five [qualities] ending with that of Indra are accomplished according to their specific distinctions.
Having practiced the fifteen desirable stages in their proper sequence,
one should master the first after three years, the next after two, and the following after one.
Within six months, or by five, four, three, two, one fortnight, or even ten or five days, [another [attains it]]. 60.
Whether by three, two, or one [of these], for one who desires them individually, the sequence is as before;
having enjoyed the desired perfection, he attains the eternal state.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the Section on the Conquest of the Elements, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. || 13 ||
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now, [we shall describe] the subtle elements (tanmātras), beginning with smell, in their proper order.
I shall fully explain the dhāraṇās for the sake of accomplishing their fruits.
The yellow [element], the subtle essence of smell, is square and measured by five joints (or, according to the Svacchanda-tantra, by five).
It resides at the tip of the nostril.
One should meditate upon [him] marked with the vajra insignia.
From the tenth day onwards, for the yogin whose mind is focused on nothing else,
a certain fragrance arrives— manifested as twofold yet appearing in many ways, though it is but a single scent. (3)
Then, within a single menstrual period, his purified scent will become stable;
after six months, he himself will consist entirely of fragrance.
Whatever fragrance pleases one in a particular place, that one applies there intensely;
within three years, one attains the accomplishment (siddhi) impelled by the five elements.
Thereafter, one should contemplate the form of the Self within the heart;
through this, one may attain the consciousness of the veil of smell in three years.
Meditating there upon that which is endowed with slight radiance and devoid of a [physical] orb,
he beholds all those who dwell in the realm of Gandhāvaraṇa.
(92) Contemplating in this very way that which resembles the reflection described in the context of the earth-principle (dharātattva),
one attains equality with it when the two [principles] have become stable as before.
Having meditated there upon his own essential nature as shining forth while situated below,
one attains lordship over that [nature] by means of the very path previously described.
Recalling everything above this in the same manner as described for the earth-principle (dharātattva),
one obtains that very form as the fruit, which resides within the veil of fragrance (gandhāvaraṇa).
Therefore, I shall now describe the concentration on the form of taste (rasa), which is practiced by yogis, by means of which the attainment of all tastes occurs for the yogi. (11)

One should contemplate the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra), which resembles a water bubble, situated at the tip of the tongue and located at the front, serving as the support for the tip of one's own tongue. 12.
With his inner self absorbed in that which is cool, possessing the six tastes, and worthy of contemplation— [as it is said: "possessing the six tastes and unctuous"]—
then, within just a month, the experience of the taste of rasa arises for him.
When, having abandoned salt and other [flavors], one has attained sweetness,
then by swallowing that, the yogi becomes a conqueror of death within six months.
Freed from old age and disease, with black hair and the undiminished luster of his youth,
he shall live as long as the moon, stars, and sun, practicing [this] here and there.
Contemplating one's own nature as having the form of a bubble described previously, what wonder is there that one attains unobscured consciousness? 16.
Meditating upon that very [reality], endowed with radiance and devoid of any support,
one shall perceive— over the course of years— the entire [world] resting within the enclosure of *rasa*.
Contemplating the reflection and other elements mentioned in the section on the water-tattva above that,
one clearly attains everything previously described arising from the enclosure of taste (rasa).

Therefore, for the sake of attaining all perfections, I shall describe the auspicious Dhāraṇā known as Rūpavatī, which bestows divine vision and rests upon the subtle element of form (rūpa-tanmātra). || 19 ||
When the yogi, staying in solitude with eyes closed,
beholds something resembling an autumnal twilight cloud— whatever it may be— [he attains the goal].
Having fixed the mind there, as long as one remains for ten days,
one perceives therein even the most subtle drops.
Some there are white, red, yellow, and others blue;
having seen them there, one whose mind is focused on nothing else should fix the mind intensely upon them.
Within six months, he sees very many forms within them;
after three years, those very forms become stable and ablaze with splendor.
By practicing those [meditations], after two years he sees them in the form of reflections;
then, after one year, he sees light; and after six months, he sees the form of a person.
Within three months, the pervasive radiance [is attained]; within one month, everything is spread forth.
And through the sequence of time, it rests upon the previously mentioned veil of form. (25)
One obtains all that fruit and divine vision arises;
thus is this meditation (dhāraṇā), free from conceptual construction, described as having been performed. || 26 ||
A fifty-fold division arises here spontaneously;
since one may reach certainty through this, what is the use of other ostentatious scriptures? (57)
Therefore, I shall now describe to you another [practice] involving touch, by means of which the yogi is born with a vajra-body. (28)
One should contemplate oneself situated within a six-cornered maṇḍala,
arid and resembling collyrium, with every limb agitated by throbbing.
Then, O Goddess, after ten days, the sensation of the touch of an ant will arise over his entire skin; then, reflecting upon that, he should continue his meditation.

Having attained the state of a vajra-body, one should obtain what was previously mentioned as before, while contemplating the previously described form in the shape of the previously mentioned maṇḍala. (31)
Who can prevent one from attaining the knowledge that veils the reality of touch? To achieve mastery over it, one should meditate upon oneself as the lower mandala. (32)
By which perfect accomplishment he shall become a perceiver of all tactile sensations,
having diligently closed his ears and closed his eyes.
When one hears that great sound, the mind should follow it there;
consequently, his digestive fire blazes up within ten days. (34)
The faculty of hearing from a distance arises after six months;
at its conclusion, a faint sound is perceived very slightly. (35)
He should be known as the soul of all; through the practice of that [meditation], with a mind focused on nothing else, one attains a stable realization that transcends the veil of words.
Furthermore, that sound which is heard at the end like the blast of a conch shell—that form of the *pralayākala* should be practiced by those desiring its fruit. (37)
When that very [principle], completely obscuring other sounds,
is called *vijñānākala*, then it is [so designated] in the Aparājita [world].
That which brings delight to the mind and is perceived at its conclusion should be known as "mantra" by yogins who desire yoga. (39)
Then, that other sound which is heard like the resonance of a peaceful bell is called Mantreśa; it bestows the fruit of all accomplishments (siddhi).
That sound which arises at the conclusion of the cessation of the bell's resonance—
For that is indeed the station of the Lord of Mantras and Lords; it is the great cause of all supernatural powers (siddhis). || 41 ||
Whatever sound a lute emits when struck by the wind,
one should know that such a resonance there is the state of Śambhu.
One should practice all of these either separately or sequentially;
thus one attains the perfection of omniscience, which relies upon the removal of the veil of sound. (43)
Thus have these five meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) upon the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) been described.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the Section on the Meditative Concentrations on the Subtle Elements, in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Now, [the functions] of the organs beginning with the organ of speech and ending with the mind are described in their proper order.
I shall now fully proclaim the eleven dhāraṇās in brief.
The wise one should contemplate the word "namaḥ" at the end of his speech as his own self;
O Madhusūdanī, by means of this silence, he attains mastery over speech.
Speech that is unimpeded in all respects proceeds forth within six months; mastery over the meaning of all treatises arises after one year. (3)
His speech shall proceed adorned with poetic ornaments;
within three years, he himself becomes a composer of treatises. (4)
Right there, one should contemplate one's own body in its proper form— furthermore, that very same body as white, slightly illuminated by a luster of light.
One should meditate upon that [light] starting from the end of the *rasa* element up to the end of the light of the lunar disc and so forth;
one gradually attains every fruit arising from the veil of speech.
And taking that [mantra] in his hand, he undoubtedly grasps an object situated at a distance of six months' journey, or even beyond the ocean after three years.
Therein, first meditating upon one's own body as resembling a lotus,
one should respectfully contemplate the fourteen [forms] according to their distinctions such as active and so forth.
By following the very path previously described and according to the previously stated rules for time,
one obtains every fruit that depends upon the repetition of the hand-gesture (*hastāvṛti*).
Meditating thus upon his feet with devotion for three years,
he wanders tirelessly across the earth bounded by the oceans in a single moment.
Having worshipped the fourteen [deities] and practiced [the meditation] upon one's own body and so forth, one obtains all the fruits as before, situated in the fourfold repetition.
Stabilizing the reality of the mind even while walking, one will without delay attain liberation from the disease of that existence within a month. || 12 ||
By reciting it for three years without negligence, one attains the status of a man of meritorious fame;
furthermore, one shall obtain here the fourteenfold fruit as previously described.
One who has conquered the senses shall remember the Liṅga by its own essential form after one month;
after six months, without effort, he shall attain the power to obtain whatever he desires.
When that fourteen-fold division has been practiced therein, the one of great intelligence obtains all the fruits arising from the covering of the *liṅga*, just as before. (15)
For ten days, the yogi should contemplate his own tongue as having the luster of the moon;
within ten days, he attains an experience arising from the tongue as if it were his own self.
One who is single-minded tastes that which is situated at a distance after six months;
after three years, he directly licks that supreme nectar. (17)
By means of this, that yogi becomes free from old age and death;
even if he is addicted to forbidden drinks and the like, he is not overcome by sins.
Contemplating everything else as before, including one's own body and so forth, one undoubtedly attains the fruit arising from the covering of the tongue. 19.
For one who gradually contemplates their own nose as having the luster of gold,
the experience of the emptiness of the nose will arise within ten days. (20)
Within six months, one will perceive the scent of even a distant object;
and by smelling the scent, one will cause the death of that person who has become wicked.
Having attained divine fragrance within three years, the knower of yoga, endowed with freedom from old age, death, and the qualities of material nature, becomes worthy of divinity.
One should contemplate everything else exactly as it has been described;
thus, abiding in the covering of the nose, one attains the gradual fruit. || 23 ||
While contemplating his own eyes, which resemble the rising sun,
he will experience a discharge of blood from his eyes for ten days.
A great pain arises on his forehead;
one should not be afraid, O Great Goddess, nor should one abandon the practice. (25)
By abandoning [this practice], one falls into blindness; therefore, one should practice it with effort.
Within six months, the great yogi becomes possessed of divine vision. (26)

The vigilant wise man perceives the earth as having fissures reaching to the edge of the iron circle (kaṭāha), and likewise, he sees everything above up to the Pole Star (Dhruva) as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand.
Within three years, the yogi perceives the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
thereafter, the knowledge of the Yoginīs residing within that body arises.
Remembering one's own body and other things previously mentioned as before, one attains everything arising from the covering of the eyes; what wonder is there in this? (29)
By recollecting his skin as being everywhere the color of collyrium leaves and free from wrinkles,
he will not be able to be slain— even by weapons— within a month.
Within six months, he is not burned even by an extremely intense fire; within three years, the yogi is not harmed by diamonds, stones, poisons, and the like.
He is never afflicted; having attained freedom from old age and death, he remains so.
Through contact, taste, smell, consciousness, and song, there are fourteen [qualities]. || 32 ||
The divisions, along with their fruits, are to be known according to the preceding time-periods;
however, in this case, one should contemplate the body as being enveloped by one's own body and so forth. (33)
The discerning practitioner, fixing his own mind upon the space of the ear,
attains the knowledge of hearing from a distance within six months.

O Goddess, he who hears all that is proclaimed within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) over the course of three years— he, being free from old age and death, clearly perceives everything in its manifest clarity.
Therein, one should contemplate everything starting with one's own body as being like the previously described ether;
one obtains all the results arising from the obstruction of the ears, just as before.
O Manovatī, I shall now describe the concentration (dhāraṇā) which bestows all perfections;
by the mastery of which, O Goddess, one obtains the fruit of all perfections. (37)
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; therefore, the practitioner of mantra should discipline it if he desires imperishable liberation. (38)
Visualizing that [form], which resembles a half-moon and is situated face-downward in the heart, one will attain intuitive insight within just one month. (39)
Suddenly one sees something, and likewise suddenly hears;
and at times and in various places, knowledge consisting of all the senses arises suddenly. (40)
For the yogi disciplined in yoga, his own respective sensory consciousness becomes perfectly clear within three years.
In this state, recollecting even one's own body and so forth as previously described,
and having attained the consciousness that removes mental obscurations, one shall obtain the quality of the moon.
Thus, you should practice these eleven songs accordingly,
since all fruit is established in the control of the senses. (43)
The wise have declared that both bondage and liberation belong to the senses;
when they are restrained, they lead to bondage, and when they are liberated, they lead to liberation. (44)
O Dear One, when these [senses] together with the mind are present within the pervasive state, they should then be known by the wise as "liberated. (45)
But when they are situated in some object located in another place, then those are said to be "bound" (baddha). || 46 ||
Thus, this twofold state—distinguished as pure and impure—is fully explained regarding the senses in the *Siddhayogīśvarīmata*. (47)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, on the Concentration on the Senses (*akṣadhāraṇā*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter. Now, [I shall describe] the divine concentration consisting of pride, the most excellent of concentrations.
O Goddess worshipped by yogis, I shall describe [the mudrā] that produces great pride for practitioners of yoga.
With undistracted mind, one should visualize a sixteen-spoked wheel within one's own body;
having contemplated "I am this," surrounded by one's own retinue.
Within three years, the yogi shall become invincible;
his sense of "mine-ness" (mamatva) shall become unshakable (acyuta) everywhere and in all circumstances.
Meditating upon his own form as the nave of such a wheel, he should contemplate: "I am everything; everything is established within me. (4)
Then, what wonder is there that he attains the consciousness of the ego (ahaṅkāra-vijñāna), while unweariedly meditating upon my own nature within the heart-center (hṛccakra)? || 5 ||
One attains the world of the Sun, which is the fruit arising from the enclosure of pride;
contemplating Nīlalohita sequentially through the entire sequence beginning with the Bimba [mandala] and so forth.
One attains everything born of that [state], impelled by the ten stages;
thus has been described the one consisting of pride (garva), which bestows the qualities of Prajāpati.
Meditating in the heart upon an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp, which is joined with the factors such as dharma and resembles the orb of the rising sun. (8)
Within one month one’s intellect becomes firm; within six months one becomes a possessor of a retentive memory;
and within three years one personally becomes an author of the scriptures.
There, one should contemplate one's own form; one perceives the principle of intellect (buddhitattva). By meditating upon Brahmā, one attains the knowledge of that Lord.
Whether sleeping or established in meditative absorption, the sage utters the seven Vedas; through constant practice, they remain clearly manifest even though they have not been studied.
Contemplating all that was previously described, beginning with the *bimba*, in due order,
one attains the sovereignty of Brahmā, which rests upon the veil of the intellect (*buddhyāvaraṇa*).
Meditating on the orb of the sun in the heart and within that the lunar disc—for him who practices in this manner, [the vision] arises after six months. (13)
Through the effortless arising of the divine eye, perfection shall be attained within three years;
by contemplating one's own body therein, one will obtain the knowledge of qualities.
Remembering the blazing form of the *liṅga*, one shall attain its lordship;
meditating on the reflection and so forth as before, [one contemplates] the tenfold group consisting of ten parts.
One undoubtedly attains the fruit situated within the veil of qualities;
these twenty-four [or, as some say, twenty] have been declared individually.
In fifteen ways. || 16 ||
The dhāraṇās of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth are beneficial for yogins in brief;
as for the other six that are established within the thirteenfold division, they are as follows: || 17 ||
These are described for yogins so that yoga may be perfected;
one should reflect that, apart from the body, there is nothing else whatsoever in its true nature. (18)
Seated upon a white lotus throne above the three mandalas—when [the visualization] has thus become stable here, the knower of yoga, within just one month, [attains stability]. 19.
What wonder is there that one becomes free from all diseases?
Within six months, his realization arises upon this earth. (20)
Freed from old age and other ailments by this [initiation], one becomes a perceiver of the reality of the Puruṣa through the three [tattvas].
Here, within the lotus below the heart, one should form a body twelve and a half finger-breadths in size.
One should meditate on one's own [deity] at the end of the heart-mantra; within six months, one becomes a conqueror of death.
Within three years, one attains equality with the Lord of the Principle of Puruṣa (puṃstattveśvara).
When all this has been contemplated there, as before, in relation to an image or other object, one obtains without doubt the fruit residing within the covering of the person. (23)
This knowledge of Vedānta has been described in brief;
formerly it was taught by Kapila, and now it has been explained by me in detail. (24)
Contemplating one's own body as resembling a mass of autumnal twilight clouds, one attains freedom from passion within six months; of this there is no doubt. (25)
Freed from old age and death, he arises after just one year;
after three years, he attains the great knowledge born of the veil of passion.
One should contemplate the body as entirely red and situated above a full cloud for six months, remaining undisturbed, in order to achieve freedom from passion.
Remembering [this] correctly for one year, one is not afflicted by death;
having conquered the pairs of opposites within three years, one attains equanimity toward passion.
Meditating upon the red [syllable] situated on a red lotus, extending five joints down to the heart,
one gradually attains the entire fruit previously described. || 29 ||
For one who repeatedly contemplates the Bimba and other [objects] mentioned previously herein, there arises the complete fruit born from the veil of passion. (30)
One should meditate upon a white lotus in the heart with sixteen petals and filaments—
divine, consisting entirely of nectar, and having the crescent moon as its pericarp.
Having restrained his mind there until it reaches the end of sleep while remaining motionless, whatever he then sees in a dream becomes true for him. (32)
For him who practices in this manner, that very fruit which has blossomed from the lotus arises in its entirety for him, through the application of the sequence of time.
Contemplating the body and so forth as being four finger-breadths [in height] everywhere in this manner, one obtains everything arising from the Vidyā-tattva, just as before. (34)
Skipping over one finger-breadth at a time from the heart,
one should meditate on three separate wheels, red, blue, and white, respectively.
Therein, the two or one parvan, as well as the Puruṣa possessing that same splendor, and whatever has been taught regarding the Bimba and so forth—this is the great triad of principles (tattva). 36.
The wise know this division to consist of thirteen parts ending with this;
now, the two principles (tattvas) are described according to their elevenfold subdivisions.
One should meditate upon one's own essential nature, situated at the navel within the five-spoked wheel that extends as far as the pit of the throat, as if perceiving it with blazing eyes.
Having fully mastered every entity that exists on the path, from the element earth up to the principle of time, the lord of yogis is no longer overcome by time. (39)
If even when an image or similar object is present there and contemplated by yogins, [the result] occurs, what wonder is there that its fruit is attained without effort? (40)
Stabilizing the mind in the space of the throat day after day,
the yogi obtains the fruit arising from Māyā even within the reflected image and so forth located there. (41)
Visualizing it as resembling the hollow of the throat, like the orb of the moon seized by Rāhu, one does not again fall under the sway of illusion and the like. 42.
Reflecting upon that very [state] there as having been liberated from Svarbhānu, one attains the nature of the Supreme Lord, including a body of light and so forth. (43)
One should contemplate the form of the entire wheel of mantras, which is their collective manifestation, as being situated on the *lambaka* and having the appearance of the midday sun. (44)
Then, through the passage of time, the yogin attains the state of a mantra;
and here, all the previously mentioned incidental fruits are also desired. (45)
Having visualized the form right there, one shall attain the state of Mantreśa;
then, having meditated on the light of the lamp below that, one shall go to its abode.
Therefore, by recollecting [the Self] as pervading all that is external and internal, as well as below and above,
a person does not fall from the state of Mantreśvara and Īśāna.
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), the yogi, recollecting the supreme seed-syllable,
should place his mind between the eyebrows, slightly in front of them.
With eyes closed and a joyful soul, in a place devoid of sound and light,
he beholds there the Puruṣa, twelve finger-breadths in height.
There, one should make the mind steady; thereafter, after three months, [one perceives] a form of light, complete in all its limbs and unwavering. (50)
With his divine eye, he beholds that serene being who resembles the moon;
having seen that divine person, the knowledge of time proceeds.
If [the mark] is on the head, death shall occur within six months;
however, the knower of yoga should there diligently practice the evasion of Time.
One should meditate upon the stainless lunar disc above the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra),
from which flows a great abundance of divine nectar that fills one's own body.
Meditating upon himself as filled from within and without by that [nectar] flowing through the stalk of the heart, he shall become a conqueror of death within ten days.
One should practice this yoga even for the destruction of a great disease,
and for the destruction of diseases affecting individual limbs, one should contemplate each limb by limb.
When one sees the color of smoke, then a great disease shall arise;
when it is black, one contracts leprosy; when blue, there is the danger of smallpox.
If the eye is defective, that disease [should be predicted]; if the nose is defective, it is of that nature;
whichever limb one cannot see, one should diagnose the disease as being located there. || 57 ||
O Īśvarī, a yogi established on the path of yoga shall, within five years, know everything up to the end of the principle of Vidyā, whether it concerns himself or others.
One knows and experiences [all] constantly, yet one is not deprived of that [state],
when the fire situated there is meditated upon as spreading through the entire body. (59)
