One attains everything previously mentioned through the application of the sequence of time;
therefore, one remains unbroken therein during the meditation on the upward-pervading [state].
Because he is the Lord of all lords of mantras, he never again returns;
thus, one should likewise contemplate the Great Radiance in the region of the forehead.
Before long, he beholds [it] endowed with eight colors in succession:
resembling sapphire, with a luster like the throat of a peacock.
Another resembles lājāvarta stone, and likewise another resembles beryl;
yet another resembles topaz, and possesses a brilliance equal to coral.
Another [vision] resembles a ruby, and another has a radiance equal to the moon;
upon seeing that supreme moonlight, divine knowledge arises. (64)
From that, everything proceeds—the movement within the monastery, walking about, and so forth.
When that which pervades above and below is meditated upon, one does not fall away from that state.
All this has been explained as established according to the distinctions of the objects to be characterized;
now, the distinction of the mind is also briefly taught. (66)

(111) With the desire for the eight qualities that culminate in the Piśāca state, one should properly fix the mind steadily upon the Lord, [visualizing] Him as possessing each of those respective forms and qualities. 67.
Thus, for this path ending with the state of the Lord (Īśvara), the various modes of worship have been explained individually for the sake of the yogis' attainment of yoga.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Section on Retention (*Dhāraṇā*), in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter:
Now, if all this that has been indicated should not attain clarity, [then...]
Once that [reality] has been made manifest and remains so, the mind clearly does not dwell there [any longer]. || 1 ||
Thereafter, one should effect the cessation of its movement by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
That is said to be fivefold, according to the divisions beginning with inhalation (pūraka). || 2 ||

Inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), exhalation (recaka), withdrawal (apakarṣaka), and the fifth, elevation (utkarṣa), should be known by yogis for the purpose of practicing that [prāṇāyāma]. || 3 ||
Pūraka is so called because of the filling of the air; it is described as being twofold and also sixfold.
One type is due to natural filling, while the other is filled after having been expelled.
It is divided by the different openings of the nostrils, mouth, and the upper palate;
thus divided, it attains a sixfold nature, which again reaches infinity through further subdivisions.

The *kumbha* (retention) is to be known as fivefold; among these, the first is that which follows inhalation (*pūraka*), and the second is proclaimed to be that which occurs after exhalation (*recaka*).
At the two ends there are two others, and the fifth abides in its own nature;
through the differentiation of various locations, this too attains infinity.
Exhalation (recaka) is to be understood as before, consisting of two types and having six aspects;
the wind, held steady in its place, is drawn upward from there.

That which is intended for the sake of reaching another location is considered "elevating" (*utkarṣaka*); that from which it is brought back again to its original place is "brought back" (*āhṛta*). (9)
These two are said to be the "subtractors" (apakarṣaka) in many ways;
one should practice them while seated in the padmaka or other postures.
The inferior [breath] is a single udghāta; the middling is considered to bestow accomplishment (siddhi);
the superior is that which has three udghātas, and it consists of twelve mātrās. || 11 ||
One should not exceed the measure of three circumambulations of the knees or the three snaps of the fingers multiplied by three, so as to avoid the afflictions of wind (vāyudoṣa). || 12 ||
One should not hold the breath in the eyes;
rather, as the vital air is gradually released while situated at the navel, heart, palate, and throat, one should maintain the concentration on each respective part.
Four dhāraṇās are to be known: Śikhī, Amvīśā, and the two whose nature is nectar (Amṛtātmikā).
Whatever substance one contemplates here, one should remember all of that as being omnipresent.
One should meditate upon the form consisting of the Bindu and Nāda, resting in the Īśānī-dhāraṇā,
and contemplate the Moon of Amṛtā according to the path described for the abandonment of time.
By means of these concentrations, the yogi established on the path of yoga,
having abandoned that which is to be discarded, shall go to the unsurpassed state.
These are considered to be the three types of eradication, numbered as three, two, and one.
By these [verses] as well, one attains the unsurpassed fruit mentioned even for the lower [levels]. || 17 ||

(114) Although the status of being a limb of yoga is equal [for all], reasoning (*tarka*) is the supreme limb of yoga. Because it consists of the investigation of what is to be abandoned and so forth, effort in that regard is praised. || 18 ||

Once the mind has become steady on the path, even though one desires to abandon the objects of the senses, one should still direct it by means of that [mind] until the state free from affliction is reached. (19)
Mental meditation is declared to be that which is joined with the contemplation of its object;
that very thing is held to be supreme knowledge consisting of contemplation. (20)
Remaining there for even a mere moment, one attains meditative absorption;
and when that too is fully perfected, one obtains the desired fruit. || 21 ||
Whatever object one contemplates does not attain a state of otherness;
having attained identity with that [object], it subsequently becomes as if non-existent.

Then the yogi, who delights the assembly of yoginīs, is as if he has reached the state of the five elements; even by intense [objects], he is not moved from his state by sound and the other [sensory objects]. (23)
Having repeatedly withdrawn the mind by this method,
one should perform all practices such as breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the sake of attaining success in yoga.
Alternatively, considering even all enjoyment to be deformed, he abandons his own body and attains the eternal state. || 25 ||
Then, one should perform the previously mentioned placement (*nyāsa*), which has a radiance equal to the fire of time (*kālānala*),
by means of the reverse procedure, [thereby attaining] the state of the pair.
Having performed the fiery concentration (āgneyī dhāraṇā) which heats all the vital points (marmans),
one should fill the body with air from the big toes up to the top of the head.
Having drawn that [vital energy] upward from the thumb, the knower of yoga should lead it to the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
he should sever all the vital points (marmans) with this mantra: 28.
Having fashioned the first Brahmin mounted on a living being and endowed with a garland of heads and so forth, one should place before him a second Brahmin who is lifeless.
Thus has been described this Kālarātri, the cutter of the vital points;
O Goddess, he who desires long life should not utter her name.
Through the practice of reciting fifty [syllables], a sensation arises at the crown of the head;
having observed this sign, one should take recourse in the meditation on Mṛtyujit.
Then, having pressed him there— one who contemplates the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth—
and having drawn him up with force, he should dispatch the Kālarātri residing therein.
From his presence, there shall arise accomplishment characterized by all that is taught for mantras.
That very [reality] is worshipped by humans in the form of mantra.
This true nature of that which is to be known has been told to you, O Goddess honored by the gods. (34)
"Even to Guha, if he is not a devotee, this must never be told by me.
It has filled his entire belly and reached as far as the aperture of Brahma. (35)
Then, by means of the practice of whirling, the yogi should likewise impel that wind until it reaches the limits of the vital breath (prāṇa), as desired by the mind of the yogis.
It is pervaded again by returning in that very same way to the navel-center.
One should practice in this manner for as long as seven days. (37)
From that time forward, being joined [with it], one may attract even the thirty gods; having attracted by means of this the wisdom (vijñāna) practiced by all yoginīs— || 38 ||
One whose self is disciplined in yoga should grasp this; what is the use of other trivial teachings?
At first, a great dizziness arises for him through practice. (39)
"Then there is trembling, O Goddess of Gods, and even subtler than that, it is as if one is blazing.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. || 17 ||
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Listen, O Goddess, to this supreme secret, unattainable by those of undisciplined souls.
That which has not been told to anyone, that I shall tell you today.
Abandoning everything else, one should fix the mind upon the mind alone;
one should not worship a linga made of clay, stone, minerals, gems, or other such materials.
One should worship the internal liṅga, wherein the moving and the unmoving are dissolved;
for it is by this that the status of being a liṅga in the external liṅga is presided over. || 3 ||
Therefore, relying upon this supreme non-duality, one should worship it with supreme meditation,
O Goddess of Gods, even by means of a single atom.
Only he who has meditated upon it perceives this liṅga, and no other;
for this which is called "vibration" (spandana) is firmly established within the heart.
Having concentrated the mind there, the knower of yoga experiences trembling and even levitation;
when that [state] has reached complete tranquility, within one month—so it is said.
O Goddess, the Liṅga has arisen from the heart and extends to the aperture of Brahmā;
it possesses stainless luster and illuminates the entirety of the body within its own light.
Therein, the one of great intelligence beholds the entire web of mantras;
having ascended its summit, he remains with undistracted mind for the duration of a month.
p.
118) Then, when that has been perfectly accomplished, all perfections arise within six months.
If a bearer of the mark (liṅgin), without understanding this mark (liṅga), should resort to a [mere external] mark, [he will fail]. || 9 ||
The exertion of such a person is in vain; he does not enjoy the fruit of the *liṅga*.
This great *liṅga* of Śiva is perfected within one's own self-constituted *liṅga*.
When this is established, it is no wonder that the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) exists within the mark (liṅga) yet is devoid of the mark; for he is characterized by that very mark. || 11 ||
When a yogin goes outside by means of this mark and the possessor of the mark, then he should be known as a "liṅgin"; the mark is held to extend to the end of the city.
From this recognition of the signs, yogins are known as "possessors of signs" (liṅgin).
By him are the mantras presided over, according to their divisions into peaceful, fierce, and so forth. (13)
What wonder is there that those whose minds have attained that state become so? If one should practice yoga by resorting to a fierce state of being, [the result follows]. 14.
He would become difficult for all—gods, asuras, and humans—to behold;
he was liberated from coming and going, and remained undaunted by any vision. 15.
For as long as he remains for even a moment, he shall attain the Lord;
possessed [by Him], he beholds everything, possessing a splendor equal to ten million suns.
Having beheld that syllable which is unmanifest, belonging to Śiva and known as Bhairava, the yogi shall attain omniscience within half a year. (17)
He who, having approached this very [state], attains satisfaction, and who is no longer involved in artificial conjunctions—he is liberated from all bonds. (18)
(119) Yogas characterized by such signs as breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and the like are considered artificial;
therefore, they do not equal even a sixteenth part of this uncreated [yoga]. || 19 ||
Practicing this with diligence, the yogi beholds divine signs;
seated upright, the yogi should not think of anything at all. (20)
In a mere moment, it would burn away everything—both the unperformed and the performed—that resides within the body;
as it is being burned, one experiences a trembling here in this world.
Then, when that [state] has become stable there, the light within shines forth;
having seen that supreme radiance, divine knowledge arises.
Even while enjoying sense objects, he attains the state of independent Śiva;
for as long as he remains for even a moment with his divine eyes unblinking.
Therefore, one realizes that the self is an all-pervading entity;
desiring the fruit of all accomplishments, one should cultivate that very state with effort. (24)
Then the yogi, trembling yet not excessively so, should meditate upon that;
thereafter, he beholds a radiance all around the tip of his forehead.
Having beheld that supreme splendor, one shall attain divine knowledge;
without effort, one succeeds within six months, and in a year, one is fully perfected.
Having become equal in power to Śiva, the knower of yoga, having made his mind all-pervading, goes wherever he desires in just a moment. (27)
One attains an immersion of power (śaktyāveśa), characterized by the experience of trembling;
then, once that has become stable there, within just one month, the knower of yoga [attains the goal]. (28)
One perceives the Śākta splendor, firm both internally and externally;
when that has been properly and perfectly accomplished, [one perceives] that which is born of all the senses with devotion.

Therein one clearly attains unimpeded consciousness; and that which is to be known here as all-pervading is that which is conjoined with the objects of the senses, yet not conjoined with them in their ultimate, imperishable nature.
This single reality alone has been declared through its various distinctions,
having set aside the entire range from the organs of action up to the intellect.
The wise one should meditate upon the supreme Śakti everywhere, having made the mind steady until he has attained identity with Her. 32.
In that moment, one attains the state that is omnipresent;
having burnt away the nets of bonds, one shall obtain the fruit as desired. || 33 ||
Therefore, having made a firm resolve within oneself, one should practice this [meditation] until the individual soul (jīva), released from its support, attains dissolution [in the Supreme]. 34.
That place is held to be the field of origin for all mantras;
it should be understood as being of two kinds, through the distinction between external and internal. (35)
That measure which is greater than what is required for the journey should be known as bestowing all accomplishments;
or else, the wise one [should proceed] for him who is traveling by means of the mode of dreaming.

One should bring about cessation for a mere moment in the middle state; there one perceives the power of consciousness (cicchakti), which lasts for only a fraction of a second (tuṭi) and is undivided. (37)
That alone is the supreme reality; from it this entire world has arisen. That indeed is the mantra-body according to the Siddhayogīśvarīmata. (38)
The mantras embraced by that very [state] bestow the fruit of all accomplishments;
its phonemes are slightly transformed, being free from both rejection and acceptance. (39)
The consciousness that one attains is called the Śiva-principle;
by making the mind steady therein, one shall attain omniscience. (40)
In that very place, one perceives divine signs without a doubt, wherever on the body a transformation arises. (41)
O Goddess, that reality preceded by volition is the supreme reality;
desiring to attain omniscience, the great yogi should practice that.
Having enjoyed his desired perfections, the yogin attains the supreme state by constantly and respectfully honoring himself with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (43)
One should worship even with devotion at the region of the *brahmarandhra*;
through the application of liquid substances, his ritual bathing (*snapana*) takes place.
The perception of the fragrance of perfumes, flowers, and so forth is considered to be worship;
the tasting of the six flavors is prepared as an offering of food (naivedya). || 45 ||
Whatever syllable one should utter, that is proclaimed to be *japa*.
Having concentrated the mind thereon, [one should perform it] while a substance is being burnt. (46)
As long as one remains within the flame, for that long the fire-oblation is considered performed;
whatever form one perceives, that very thing is intended as meditation. || 47 ||
In this context, this great non-dual sacrifice has been indicated:
one should fix the mind steadily at the upper aperture, possessing a radiance like the rising sun;
or one should do so likewise in the heart, or else one may attain it at the *dvādaśānta*.
Then, within half a month, that very form is perceived.
Having mastered that which has been perceived, it conduces to omniscience;
covering his face with a cloth, the yogi should fix himself upon the object of focus. (50)
From the bulbous root of the navel downwards, as far as the principle (tattva) ending at the crest-lock,
it resembles a subtle star and is made formidable by the flames of its rays.
But at the cessation of the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti), one beholds the form of the Self;
O Goddess, for one who practices that very [form], it attains full expansion.
That face of all mantras is recited in all tantras;
therefore, some realization of it is expected within just one month.
Since it knows everything established within the heart,
having realized that [knowledge], the yogi should not impart it correctly to anyone.
One should perform the recitation from the chapter [only] at the proper time; otherwise, one shall meet with untimely death.
Even after dying, one is cooked in succession within the multitude of hells. (55)
Knowing this, O Great Goddess, one should acquire what is for one's own welfare;
even a disciple who receives [teachings] through improper means falls into hell.
And at that time, my word does not fail;
having attained knowledge through right reasoning, one does not subsequently fall back from it.
Then the wise one, a knower of yoga, having meditated upon him and established him in his own essential form as if standing before him, should perform the extraction of his consciousness. 58.
One should arrange the sixfold path within his body as previously described;
then, having observed that lamp at the tip of his big toe in sequence, [one should proceed]. (59)
Having withdrawn the splendor [of the disciple] with one-pointed mind to the dvādaśānta,
he should then contemplate it there as having attained oneness with Śiva.
There, one should meditate upon the form of darkness, which has the nature of causing concealment;
by that path, [one should visualize the soul] falling until it reaches the tip of the big toe.
One should meditate upon [the deity] as being both external and internal, radiant and like thick collyrium;
by this method, for that dull-witted and evil-souled person, [the result follows]. 62.
Consciousness, mantras, spells, and the like do not provide assistance;
for [the result] arises through the mere intention of the mind, even when [the object] is unseen. 63.
Or else, having visualized in front of oneself that which has somehow been perceived as a constant source of harm, or as resembling the orb of the sun, it should be severed. 64.
One should contemplate him as being seized by the power in the form of Svarbhānu,
filled with great wrath on account of thousands of offenses. (65)
One should perform this rite for the sake of play, but never otherwise;
for one who has fallen away from this rite through another [means] is deprived of higher knowledge.
It cannot be joined again as long as it has not been extracted by that very same [agent];
however, one whose mind is drawn by compassion, having performed its purification, [may do so]. || 67 ||
Then, after [the disciple has performed] penances prescribed by rule through sacred fords such as breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and so forth,
one should perform his initiation according to the previously mentioned method.
Therefore, one who has no other thought obtains all that fruit;
having understood this, the wise person should strive diligently to attain Garuḍa.
Since contentment has arisen, consisting of the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva,
one should not investigate his conduct, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
He alone discerns whether that [action] is appropriate or indeed inappropriate, when he is attached to improper deeds that rob one of life and wealth. (71)
Then he should be restrained by the wise man with a bow;
yet, even while being thus restrained by him, if he does not desist, [the following should be done]. || 72 ||
Then, having gone elsewhere to some place, one should contemplate Śiva alone.
This method of yoga has been declared in brief for the benefit of yogins. (73)
Herein there is neither purity nor impurity, no consideration of what is fit to be eaten and so forth;
there is neither duality nor even non-duality, and no worship of external symbols and the like.

Furthermore, neither the renunciation of those things, nor the state of being without possessions, nor even the state of possessing possessions— such as the gathering of matted hair, ashes, and so forth— is [the cause]. (75)

The renunciation of those [worldly things], as well as the performance and non-performance of vows and other observances, the entering of sacred sites (kṣetra) and so forth, and the preservation of the rules of conduct (samaya) and so on—[these constitute the practice]. (76)
In this [state], neither the nature, marks, and so forth of another, nor name, lineage, and so forth, are prescribed, nor are they prohibited in any way. (77)
In this regard, everything may be prescribed, or likewise, everything may be prohibited;
however, O Goddess of the Gods, this alone is enjoined here as a mandatory rule.
The yogi should stabilize the mind upon reality with great effort;
and in whatever way that [stabilization] may occur for him, he should practice accordingly. (79)
But one whose mind is unwavering in reality, even while enjoying sense objects,
is not touched by defects, just as a lotus leaf is not touched by water.
Just as one who is protected by mantras and the like that remove poison does not lose consciousness even while consuming poison, so too is the yogi of great intelligence. 81.
Thus has this been told, O Goddess; what else do you wish to ask?
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Supreme Vidyā," in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.
Then, having heard this supreme method of yoga, the daughter of Śaṅkara—
Again, with a serene countenance, she prostrated before the Teacher of the World and spoke.
O Lord, Mālinī, whose source is distinct, has been heard as that which is to be accomplished;
and the triad of Vidyās, together with their ancillaries, has been duly determined.
Now I truly desire to hear how non-duality is established;
out of favor toward the best of practitioners, you should explain this for their benefit. (3)
Thus addressed by Maheśānī, the Lord of the worlds,
his lotus-face blossoming with joy, respectfully replied with nectar-like words.
Desiring to propitiate Śambhu according to the method declared in the Kula tradition,
the wise one should first worship the Kulacakra by the path prescribed for initiation.
Then one should recite the supreme Śakti mantra one hundred thousand times without interruption,
enclosed within the seed-syllables of Parā, neither too fast nor too slow.

In the same way, one should recite its eight fragments a hundred thousand times each, and one hundred thousand times for the unfragmented [root mantra], as well as six hundred thousand times for Kuleśvara, with undistracted mind.
Having offered the previously mentioned substance ten times [the number of recitations],
the wise one who is habituated to the constant mindfulness [of the deity] attains perfection of speech.

O Goddess, for one who is devoted to recitation within their own lineage, even if they lack the power to accomplish [the supreme goal], there arise in this world the riches of enjoyment, O Goddess, as the youngest [or: the maiden goddess]. (9)
One who is capable may achieve middling or even supreme accomplishment;
having performed the rite of service, he should wander the earth like a leaf blown by the wind.
He should stay for five nights in a city, but for three nights in a port town.
And having stayed even for a single night in a village, one should perform this rite.
The first letter of the name of whatever object—whether it be a city or anything else—is declared by those who know the ritual rules to be its *kula*; of this there is no doubt. (12)
Whichever deity is established as the one to be expressed within a particular group, that very deity should be meditated upon and worshipped by practitioners as its presiding lord. (13)
Having approached some city or similar location with devotion,
and having established himself in his own directional sector, he should apply the wheel at its own rising.
When each one has arisen in this manner, the deity is Māheśvara. || 15 ||
Just as [one meditates] at night in sequence, so too during the day;
the wise one should contemplate that very same group in its own direction upon its own rising.

One should remain until the next [deity] arises, and then take refuge in one's own direction; either while contemplating one's own family (*kula*) according to the rule, or else [contemplating] that very region and family. (17)
The mantra-practitioner should then contemplate another direction in that same manner, proceeding by the path described for the wheel of families (kulacakra) until he reaches his own place. 18.
Having wandered about, she returns again according to her previous sequence;
having arrived thus, O Goddess of Gods, she becomes the mistress of that region and family. 19.
He should give some food and other such items, or have them given by someone else;
thus engaged according to this rule, he maintains secret conduct and remains firm in his vow. 20.
Having attained union with the Yoginīs, one achieves perfection in just six months;
yet, O Goddess, this rite is difficult for base men who lack spiritual essence to perform.
He is the foremost bringer of all accomplishments in all the Kula scriptures.
Now, even in a single village, town, or city— || 22 ||
Resorting to that particular direction, one should thus recite this family-mantra;
without effort, one shall achieve the supreme fruit within three years.
Having abandoned worldly affairs and accepting only a single morsel of food,
one should instead meditate upon the wheel of the family-nature within the navel-center.
One should perform mental circumambulation according to the sequence of all times;
then, within half a year, the assembly of Yoginīs will reach the end of his body.
It manifests without doubt as the illuminator of one's own consciousness;
by that mere manifestation, the yogi becomes a noble member of the family of yogis. (26)
O Goddess, Supreme Sovereign, he may even become the husband of yogis;
or else, O Goddess, he should contemplate the group of eight beginning with the letter Ya. (27)
Meditating upon Kuleśāna, who makes himself known through his own nature, with a form agitated and formidable by radiance, one should contemplate him in the center of that [mandala]. (28)
And the yogi, desiring the station of the Yoginīs, should contemplate that entire wheel as having subsequently become the shape of a lamp-flame. (29)
When this has attained manifestation, it is called "established in the body" (piṇḍastha);
from that, O Goddess, the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) arises for him spontaneously. (30)
O Goddess worshipped by the immortals, passion, heroism, compassion, sorrow, anger, and so forth— this is designated as the awakened state, known as "residing in the body" (piṇḍastha).
Then, for him who is thus engaged, after many days,
the realization of the essential natures of the principles beginning with Earth arises.
They desire that supreme knowledge, which is established in the body (piṇḍastha), to be well-awakened;
and one should then contemplate the wheel there, having three spokes and eight corners.
Enveloped by the letters from *ka* to *ha*, with its original form and the *bindu*, one who performs everything there as before shall obtain this fruit. (34)
Or else, the yogi, recollecting the sixteen-spoked [wheel] joined with the first letter,
or by the middle sequence, [attains] the fifth [state] through the Cumbaka and other [breaths].
There are seventy-two thousand channels in the navel-cakra;
because they attain the state of a single mass (piṇḍa) therein, it is called "the mass" (piṇḍa). || 36 ||
That which is to be known as abiding therein is declared to be "piṇḍastha" (established in the body),
which is stainless and free from hair and so forth.
One attains freedom from fever by chance within a year;
for this group of five wheels is situated in the heart as before. (38)
The wise declare that the "pada" (word) has four divisions;
O Goddess, that place where the comprehension of meaning occurs is called a pada.
In this matter, a fourfold division consisting of fifteen parts is to be understood;
through the perfect accomplishment of the *sarvatobhadra*, one attains the state of being auspicious in every respect.
Freed from the defects of old age and death, the contemplator of yoga,
even while pervasion is well-established, has as his domain the reality that lies beneath illusion.
He perceives his equality with that Lord and attains lordship over him;
however, while established in the state, he should not contemplate [the self] as having the luster of the moon or the luster of a lamp. (42)
What wonder is there that this very [practice], when meditated upon, fills one's own body with a flood of nectar and brings about the destruction of death? (43)
This which has been described, beginning with the lunar disc, is merely an illustration;
for in whatever form the Supreme Goddess is meditated upon, [she is that]. (44)

Through these various manifestations, such as Piṇḍastha and others, she bestows the desired fruits; those who wish for the sovereign form of Śiva, the destroyer of the sword [of suffering], desire her.
(131) Because that which is situated between the eyebrows is established therein,
the pentad, resembling the sun and abiding in form, is so designated. || 46 ||

In that case as well, O Mistress of the Gods, the accomplishment arising from the stages ending with Īśvara is as previously established; however, that which transcends form has already been explained in many ways.
Thus, this supreme pervasion of the wheel of the Kula has been briefly explained for the sake of all accomplishments, according to the Siddhayogīśvarīmata.

Always, or else according to their distinctions and through the differentiation of separate phonemes, [this is taught] for the sake of the complete accomplishment of all vidyās and so forth for yogins who desire yoga. (49)
Furthermore, the distinction of castes is proclaimed according to the oral tradition:
one should meditate upon her in the heart in the form of a woman, adorned with white garments and the like.
Seated upon the navel-cakra, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons,
that which is the seed-syllable of all scriptures shall then manifest incessantly.
One should contemplate it as it issues forth from one's own mouth,
having the form of a string of pearls, filled with shimmering rays of light.
Commenced with syllables resembling stars, it possesses immeasurable splendor;
within half a month, it unceasingly disgorges a compendium of scriptures.
Established in samādhi, one may [recover] within a month in a dream, or within six months at will;
even those scriptures that have been lost, whether in their textual form or their meaning.
If the yogin has attained identity with that [object], he knows it even after a year;
this has been described in brief as a secondary result. (55)
The attainment of equality with the Vidyeśvaras and other supernatural powers (siddhis) are now described according to their specific distinctions for each individual phoneme.
This should be meditated upon constantly by yogins desiring those respective fruits,
according to the threefold path through the application of the sequence of placement (vinyāsa).

The knower of yoga, having established in its very own form that letter which arises from the power of the [respective] family and resides in whichever limb, should concentrate upon it right there. (58)

Making the darkness vanish by its shimmering mass of light, it makes the mind steady here, precisely through the sequence of prior time, by means of the path described for the practice of reality. 59.
One obtains every supreme fruit born from the pervasion of its colors;
or else, someone may employ it in rites such as subjugation (vaśya) and the like.
Then it quickly fulfills the desired aim of the practitioner—the entire sequence of syllables, which possesses the luster of the rising sun. (61)
With this desire, one should meditate for seven days upon this golden-hued river of wine flowing repeatedly, [placing it] in all the limbs of the person [being treated] in due order.
Having become submissive like a slave, he desires no other master;
she is endowed with the beauty of the three and seven [marks], her eyes wandering across her lotus-like feet.
By this very procedure, one may bring even Urvaśī without effort, let alone a mortal woman, [or a woman] who has gone to the cities of Vāyu or Agni. (64)
She should be known as the attractor of the *piṇḍa* even from hundreds of *yojanas*;
she is joined with the luster of the full moon in autumn. 65.
When properly installed in its own place, it bestows incomparable peace upon oneself or another; it resembles molten gold. (66)
O Daughter of Śaṅkara, within ten days alone it bestows great nourishment,
appearing like the juice of the rose-apple fruit and resembling a diamond peg.
In the rite of piercing, the yogi should contemplate [the deity] as being like a parrot’s plumage; in the rite of deluding, she resembles a blue diamond and cuts through every location. 68.
One should meditate on her, whose touch is like the fire of cosmic destruction, for the sake of destroying enemies;
she who is desired by those terrified by the rod of the garland,
and who resembles the mountain of the Kula.
One should visualize her as resembling smoke and utterly agitated by fire,
even when recollecting her for the pacification of anger, as prescribed for rites of pacification (śāntika).
In the rite of heating (tāpana), however, the wise man should likewise visualize her form as being like the sun;
in the rite of creating enmity (vidveṣa), she is like a dove, and in the rite of breaking (bhañjana), she resembles a blue jay.
In the case of consumption, one should visualize [the deity] as blue, green, yellow, red, or black;
when a disease arises in a specific limb, one should visualize it as arising from that very same [limb]. (72)
The yogin should contemplate the color according to the path described for the rite of slaying;
likewise, he should do so according to the path described for the rite of pacification in order to bring about its tranquility. (73)
One should contemplate [this] whether in a collection of acquired diseases or even those innate;
or else, some who desire the perfection of speech (vāksiddhi) should recite this mantra. (74)
Then, according to this procedure, one should prepare a rosary made from gems, pearls, conch shells, lotus seeds, and so forth. (75)
Or else, a wise person should fashion one made of gold or other metals, measuring fifty finger-breadths,
so that it becomes a bracelet fitting the circumference of one's own forearm.
Having taken that [flower], having anointed it and perfumed it with incense and fragrance, and having worshipped the Lord of the Family (kuleśāna), one should place the Śakti there. || 77 ||
One should utter each seed-syllable individually, enclosed within the seed-syllables of Parā;
then, one should join them with the radiating letter *KṢĀṂ* into a single initial syllable. (78)
One should again contemplate the primordial syllable as all-pervasive and the presiding authority over everything;
for this rule is intended for both varieties of the division of phonemes.
One should place the second pervasive syllable in the second [position] as before;
this same procedure is desired for the third and subsequent syllables ending with *pha*.
Then, recollecting Śakti with a one-pointed mind,
he should visualize her as having the luster of a thread situated in the center of the beads for the sake of consecrating the rosary.
One should cause her to revolve like a wheel; whatever one speaks here, all that is fashioned as recitation for the sake of the complete accomplishment of the mantra. (82)
In the same way, there should be an oblation when the consecrated person is being burned;
if, however, one should cause it to revolve while enraged by employing the ritual in reverse, [the following occurs].
The *nadā* mantra slays the enemy along with his servants, forces, and vehicles;
for whatever rite the practitioner performs here, he accomplishes it by means of mental concentration after having consecrated it with mantras. (84)

At night, O Goddess, one should rotate the rosary here according to the divisions beginning with Saumya; that very [rosary] becomes perfected for one who has performed the ritual of service, O Beloved.
And here, service consists of rotating the rosary for six months;
for the yogin engaged in this rite, [the goal is attained] after three years.
O Goddess, the perfection of speech arises, which is very difficult for all the worlds to obtain;
there is never any other perfection on earth superior to the perfection of speech. (87)
Since speech consists of phonemes and Mālinī has the form of phonemes, or else the wise one should contemplate her as having the shape of a flaming torch. 88.
Then, she emerged from her own body,
flashing forth with a continuous stream of sparks numbering in the tens of millions, filled with radiant rays.
Whether it be a village or a town, a city or even a country; a province, the entire earth, or even the whole cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 90 ||
Or, having pervaded the vast multitude of people, each one of whom is most excellent,
he returns again after having filled both the exterior and the interior.
One should remember her entering one's own body with her former form; thus one should practice day after day with an inner self absorbed in that. (92)
Then, within just a month, the people residing there came to that sacred ford (tīrtha), their strength and splendor augmented by Śakti’s power.
Formed women of various appearances, such as *lalanā* and others, as well as those who roam the earth, undergo agitation within six months; of this there is no doubt. (94)
O Great Goddess, the Nāyikās born from the womb, those born from the field, and those arisen from the sacred seats (pīṭha), become agitated in succession after one year. || 95 ||

Those [energies] situated in the intermediate space, those divine ones, and those residing in the world of Brahmā—all those within the cosmic egg undergo agitation through the three measures (mātrās). || 96 ||
Each bestows her own consciousness as desired by the practitioner;
if they do not grant what is desired by the practitioner, [the rite proceeds]. 97.
Divine wisdom perishes and the lineage is severed when the desired fruit is requested with devotion by the preeminent practitioner after having given [the gift]. 98.
Having fulfilled the commands of their gurus, they shall attain unsurpassed perfection;
having acquired wisdom from them, the yogi becomes a noble member of the family of yogis.
Having enjoyed pleasures as they desire, they attain the supreme state;
thus has this excellent Kaulika rite been described in brief. (100)
For the sake of all accomplishments of the yogins who follow the path of the Kula. || 101 ||
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, concerning the Wheel of the Kula, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. 19.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Next, the Śākta consciousness is described through the distinctions of the *piṇḍa* (syllabic body) and so forth.
This is for the sake of the yogis' accomplishment of yoga, in brief and not in detail.
The term *piṇḍa* is said to mean "body"; likewise, it refers to the nature of Śakti and Śiva. It is also celebrated as the bliss of Brahman, strength, splendor, virility, and vital energy.
That [power] of the Self, though beginningless, is obstructed by ignorance;
for the sake of its manifestation, everything that is unobstructed proceeds forth. || 3 ||
Manifested by that [power], and abandoning its previous state, it attains those consciousnesses which have been described below. (4)
They desire that very state from which the comprehension of all objects arises;
therefore, it is eternally produced from the eternal Śiva and the Self.
That very form is said to belong to the self, yet it is perishable;
they call that which transcends form the supreme, beyond the reach of the senses.
Having paid homage to the teacher, the wise one should practice its cultivation;
he should contemplate the object until the state free from affliction is reached. (7)
It is not thus, nor is it not thus; it is neither thus, nor even is it not thus—clearly, by means of a mind disciplined in yoga, until this [realization] is fully sufficient. (8)
Having made oneself identical with that [state], free from all sense objects and faculties, one remains for a moment; as long as one stays thus, trembling arises. (9)
There may also arise dizziness, sleepiness, and a slight sense of bliss;
one should apply the mind there with effort, desiring the supreme fruit.
This very form of the Self has been made manifest by Śiva;
yet, wherever it may be, it should be understood as existing as the essence of Śiva.
One should ascertain that [the Self] exists as the strengthener of that [subtle form], by constantly practicing that [meditation] while relying upon gross bodies and the like. (12)
Though inherently undivided, it attains a fourfold division through devotion;
in the gross body, it is said to be twofold, by way of the external and internal distinctions. (13)
They maintain that there are two [bodies]: the first is material and external, and the second is the subtle body (ativāhika).
In this regard, by relying upon the first, the yogin clearly perceives even those things that possess consciousness.
He fully grasps external objects and even some internal ones;
through reliance on the second [stage], he attains the objects that are the true nature of reality. || 15 ||
And he clearly perceives within his own body the sacred seats (pīṭhas), fields (kṣetras), and so forth;
whatever arises for him from this contemplation of his true nature [is the result]. (16)
By steadying the mind there, one obtains all of that very thing;
therefore, one should not perform this [practice] elsewhere out of a desire for the highest goal.
Freed from the two aggregates (piṇḍa), yet still possessed of some residual impression (vāsanā) of them,
and abiding within the state of pure consciousness alone (vijñānakevala), it is designated as the "stage" (pada). || 18 ||
Having reached this state through the application of the sequence of consciousness, one attains the state of super-consciousness that transcends the arising of form. || 19 ||
This fourfold [classification] is to be known as being based on the fourfold reliance upon the object;
and that [reliance] is preceded by the realization of reality and so forth, and has its limit in falling away from it. (20)
Since the state of one's own true nature, being free from the condition of the word and yet slightly following it, is that which brings about its manifestation. (21)
That which is endowed with that [form] is called "situated in form" (rūpastha) because of its similarity to it;
and that too has been described as being of four kinds, according to the distinctions of "arisen" (udita) and so forth.
And through the arising of knowledge, O Goddess of gods, that [practice] yields its fruit because of the sense of "mine-ness.
By this sequential yoga, one should fix [the mind] within those who are in between.
The mind attains purity, the supreme state that transcends form;
that too is said to be fourfold, according to the distinctions in the fruit of realization.
Having practiced those three kinds [of yoga] with the desire for the fruit of all supernatural powers,
one abandons the body after the fourth [birth] and is liberated at that very moment.
Thus has the knowledge of Śiva been illustrated through the divisions of the piṇḍa and so forth;
now hear the collection of mantras and vidyās according to the rules for the practice of yoga. (26)
(140) Arrayed according to the previously stated procedure, in the location previously enjoined,
one should contemplate the supreme syllable somewhere within the five locations beginning with the navel. (27)
By its own nature, it shone with light, illuminating the interior of its body;
then, by its intense radiances, [the light] extended as far as the world of Brahmā.
O beloved, as he thus remembers, after seven days a very great immersion into the power of Rudra arises within him.
Possessed, he utters many sentences in Sanskrit and other languages, as well as loud laughter, singing, and even the howling of jackals. (30)
But with his mind possessed, he does not know anything at all;
when released after a month, wherever he looks, [he sees that very thing]. || 31 ||
In each of those directions, he beholds all the quarters filled with rays;
whichever direction he gazes upon for six months, it remains so joined [with light].
One perceives various forms within each of those [states];
one should not fix the mind upon them, nor should one abandon practice. || 33 ||
A yogin performing such [a practice] becomes timid or insane;
however, even while remaining absorbed in that state, a hero regains his power through heedfulness.
Within a year, one attains the perfection of yoga desired by the mind—
whether it be the supreme, the intermediate, or the lower, according to one's wish.
One should meditate upon the true being of the assembly of Mothers, or the heart of Bhairava, or even Navātman, or indeed Ratiśekhara himself. (36)
Or else, there may be the eight [mantras] beginning with Aghorī, or those beginning with Māheśī;
or the Rudras distinguished by Amṛta and so forth, or even the Śaktis.
All are said to be equal in power, having arisen from the energy (śakti) of Rudra;
or else, the supreme distinction among those filled with nectar is now described.

One should fashion the mantra as the Vidyā, with the *prāṇa* (the letter *ha*) situated [at the beginning], surmounted by *parā* (the letter *kṣa*), and each [syllable] illuminated; it is the seat of *parā*, with the *prāṇa* (*ha*) surmounting it. (39)
O Goddess, one should meditate upon a wheel of twelve spokes, or sixteen spokes,
or eight spokes, or even three hundred spokes.
Now listen to how everything is for the six-spoked [cakra] as well;
this has been explained in brief, along with two hundred and fifty cakras.

This [state] attains a threefold nature through the distinction between female, male, and their union (yāmala); and through the distinction of rites such as pacification (śānti) and others, it attains twelvefoldness in each case. (42)
Dakṣa, Caṇḍa, Hara, Śauṇḍī, Pramatha, Bhīma, Manmatha, Śakuni, Sumati, Nanda, Gopāla, and then Pitāmaha. || 43 ||
Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Kālī, Karālī, Vikṛtānanā, Kroṣṭakī, Bhīmamudrā, Vāyuvegā, and Hayānanā. (44)
Gambhīrā and Ghoṣaṇī—these twelve are proclaimed [as the goddesses].
O Dear One, those beginning with Brahmāṇī likewise occupy the four corners starting from Āgneyī. (45)
Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Lakṣmī, Dīpti, Mālā, Śikhā, Śivā, Sumukhī, Vāmanī, Nandā, Harikeśī, and Hayānanā. (46)
Viśveśī, Sumākhyā (or Sāmākhyā), and these others—these twelve [deities] in sequence;
their designators should be known as the vowels, excluding the neuter ones. || 47 ||
In the sixteen-spoked [cakra], there are Amṛtā and the others according to the divisions of the recitation among women;
[and] Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Śarvarīśvara.
Argheṣa, Bhārabhūti, Sthiti, Sthāṇu, Hara, Jhiṇṭhīśa, Bhautika, and likewise the other, Sadyojāta. || 49 ||
Anugraheśvara, Krūra, and Mahāsena are the sixteen;
then Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Dhṛti.
Dīpti, Puṣṭi, Mati, Kīrti, Saṃsthiti, Sugati, Smṛti,
and Suprabhā as the sixteenth— these are the powers (śaktis) beginning with Śrīkaṇṭha.
In the sixteen-spoked [cakra], the vowels are to be known everywhere as the denoters;
likewise, in the eight-spoked [cakra], the deities beginning with Aghora and those beginning with Aghorī are located.
O Goddess, listen now to these twenty-four [goddesses], beginning with Māheśī;
likewise, all those beginning with Nandā in their proper order, as well as those beginning with Brahmāṇī. (53)
Saṃvarta, Lakulīśa, Bhṛgu, Śveta, and Baka;
Khaḍgī, Pinākī, and Bhujaga— the ninth is Dālin, being of such a kind.
And Bali alone. || 54 ||
Mahākāla, Dviraṇḍa, Chhagalāṇḍa, and Śikhin;
likewise Lohita, Meṣa, and Mīna, as well as those named Tridaṇḍi and Āṣāḍhi. (55)
Umākānta, Ardhanārīśa, Dāruka, Lāṅgulī, as well as Someśa and Śarmā—these twenty-four are considered [the forms]. (56)
The letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *bha* are to be known as being on the eight-spoked [wheel], while the group of eight beginning with *ya* is also there;
the letter *ma*, existing in the form of a *bindu*, stands above them all. (57)
Then, in the six-spoked [cakra], according to the sequence of the six, are Juṃkāra and likewise Svāhā;
and Bali, Balinanda, Daśagrīva, Hara, and Haya. (58)
And Mādhava, O Great Goddess, is proclaimed as the sixth;
likewise Viśvā, Viśveśvarī, Hārādrī, and Vīranāyikā. (59)
The Yoginīs are remembered as six by means of those very seed-syllables, beginning with Ambā and Gurvī;
all of them are mutually entwined according to the distinction between the Lord and the enclosures.
The letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' bestow the fruit of all accomplishments upon yogins and practitioners of mantra who are engaged in meditation and worship. (61)
Alternatively, by reciting and meditating upon whichever vidyā or previously mentioned mantra one desires from among all the cakras, one attains success.

Thus has been briefly proclaimed that which bestows the fruit of all desires. Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Determination of All Mantras," in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*. 20.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter:
Hereafter, [I shall explain] the supreme secret, the most excellent nectar of the knowledge of Śiva.
It is described for the sake of destroying disease and death for practitioners of yoga. || 1 ||
In the sixteen-spoked wheel of the sky-farer, whose pericarp is fashioned from the moon,
one should meditate upon Parā there, who flows as nectar in her own essential form.
Having been armored by the previous nyāsa, the wise practitioner should remain thus for a moment;
then, having brought the tongue [to its proper state], he should apply it to the pendant [necklace].
One should visualize the divine nectar flowing, white as the orb of the moon;
his mouth becomes filled with a little salt water.
Because of its iron-like smell, one should not drink it there, but should rather discard it;
one should practice this in this manner until it becomes sweet.
By drinking that, one is thereafter born free from old age and disease;
within six months, without effort, one becomes a conqueror of death within a year.
Once a delicious taste has arisen there, from that moment on,
whatever substance he thinks of while going there, his mouth is filled with it.
Blood, or wine, or fat, or even milk;
or ghee, oil, and so forth—whatever liquid substance [he offers], with undistracted mind. (8)
Now I shall fully explain another supreme procedure for transference:
by means of the science of yoga, one may enter a dead body while it is still alive.
Standing in a windless place, having conquered the vital breaths and mastered the sequence of postures,
one should gradually effect the entry of the air into a cotton tuft from the sun.
One should perform the ritual of attraction through taste (*svādākṛṣṭi*) using jaggery and neem as far as necessary;
then, having fashioned an auspicious image with sandalwood, jaggery, and camphor.
Placing the straight [needle] upon the secondary parts of the limbs that lack [the primary] qualities,
even after making the deposit there, one should perform the piercing very gradually.
One should effect cessation therein, and immediately after that, the "stirring" (ghaṭṭana).
This "stirring" should be understood as the movement of the limbs and the minor members [of the body]. (13)
As that yogi, disciplined in yoga, practices in this manner,
the image wavers and even runs directly toward him.
One should push it again until it has returned to its natural position;
once it has fallen, one should move it again, whether it is lying face up or on its side. (15)
In this way, as long as the entire self has attained independence,
from that point onward, the yogi may enter wherever he pleases.
Whether in a corpse or a living body, by means of the distinction between *saṃkrānti* and *ākānti*,
one should cast the net of power (*śaktijāla*) like water into all the joints of the limbs. (17)
The wise one should assail his power limb by limb;
he should protect his own body, otherwise, upon being assailed, he would perish. (18)
When one becomes firm in the aim, then, even while simultaneously relinquishing them, one undoubtedly assumes many bodies at once.
Now I shall further proclaim the divine nectar of meditative absorption, which produces immediate conviction and destroys the death of yogis. (20)
Known as "Moon-Attracting," it bestows the enjoyment of yoga within a month;
on the second day of the bright fortnight, when the sun is situated in Aries.
Having bathed, being pure, abstaining from food, and having performed the rites of worship,
the wise one should place the collection of lunar digits presided over by the Supreme Goddess.
Established in a place free from all disturbances, the wise man, with a one-pointed mind and a tranquil self, is permeated by the true being of Śiva. || 23 ||
One should gaze at the moon until it has set;
thereafter, one should eat with milk while remaining absorbed in meditation upon the moon.
In this manner, one should perform [the practice] day by day until the fifteenth day arrives;
for the remainder of the night, one should sleep while meditating upon the Supreme Goddess as residing within the lunar orb.
Likewise, on the full moon day, the yogin, having arrived at midnight when the people have become silent and all living beings are fast asleep, [should practice]. (26)
Resembling ten million moons, adorned with strings of pearls,
clad in white garments, and anointed with white sandalwood paste.
Adorned with pearl ornaments, beautiful, and in the bloom of youth,
she is the goddess who brings nourishment, streaming nectar from all sides.
And he beholds the supreme goddess seated upon a lotus throne, established in yogic sleep within the lunar orb; of this there is no doubt. (29)
Then, having pervaded her with his mind, the wise one should draw her in until she reaches the tip of his mouth, and there he should make his mind steady.
Then, having opened his mouth with a mind intent on meditation,
he should swallow it after drawing it in, and contemplate it once more within his heart.
Once she has entered his body, the yogi becomes free from suffering;
having attained strength equal to that of Śakti, he shall live as long as the moon and stars endure.
Though he is one, by his own will he divides himself into many forms;
thus, having brought the three worlds under his control, he enjoys them all simultaneously.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures until the time of dissolution arrives,
he attains the supreme Nirvāṇa, which is difficult to attain for those who have not performed meritorious deeds.
Alternatively, if one is unable to contemplate that [deity] in the sky,
one should meditate on the reflection in water and so forth, as before. (35)
Having drunk that with the mind, one should sleep while recollecting the remainder;
within six months, one attains in its entirety what was previously described.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Attraction of the Moon," in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*. 21.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Furthermore, O beloved, I shall tell you another supreme secret.
This unsurpassed nectar of yoga has not been told to anyone.
This practice, named "The Attraction of the Sun," bestows the perfection of yoga upon practitioners;
it is fully accomplished in exactly four months and eight days.
One-eighth of a *prahara* is called a *nāḍikā*;
one should practice [this] every day, increasing by one-quarter of that [unit] at each step.
In a secluded place where the sun is visible from sunrise until sunset, and which is free from all disturbances; || 4 ||

Having fasted for a day and night when the sun is situated in Capricorn, the yogi, having become pure, performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), and taken measures against the cold, [should proceed]. || 5 ||
One should place upon the solar disc a wheel with eight, six, or twelve spokes,
accompanied by Śiva, Śakti, and the Gaṇas, and joined with the eight Bhairavas.

One should contemplate the eight-spoked [wheel] within the image, conjoined with the seasons beginning with the rainy season and associated with the months, constellations, and so forth; one should contemplate the remainder within the rays.
Having concentrated the mind there and desiring to speak at the prescribed time,
one should gaze at the orb of the sun with eyes unblinking.
Then, after some time has passed, with his eyes well-closed,
he shall enter a world of darkness that is free from all affliction.
There, with eyes opened, one perceives the form of the reflection;
having fixed consciousness upon that, one should remain until one no longer sees.
Even when the mind has perished, one should remain for the remainder of the time recollecting [the object];
in this way, O Goddess of the Gods, through the noose (pāśa), that [object] becomes firmly established.
Within two months, one perceives everything; of this there is no doubt. Within three months, one beholds everything filled with the solar orb.
When the sun has entered Taurus at the conclusion of the prescribed time,
he beholds the Supreme Lord together with his discus within the solar orb.
Having drawn in what has been perceived, one should bring it to stability within the fire of the mouth;
having drunk it as before, one should afterwards bring the activity to a state of immobility.
There, O Goddess of gods, as soon as he remains for a moment having unified himself with that [deity], he abandons the earth.
While the multitude of people looks on, he goes together with the sun;
by this method, O Goddess, he becomes a lord of the masters of perfected yoga.
From Śiva down to the earth, it is nowhere obstructed;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, one merges into the partless Supreme.
This very wheel of the Khecarīs, wherein one attains the state of moving through the sky, has been proclaimed along with its secret in the *Siddhayogīśvarītantra*. (18)
Alternatively, for one of firm resolve who first contemplates their own body, both internally and externally, in the form of a wheel, the fruit shall certainly be attained. (19)
Or, pronouncing [the mantra] beginning with *pha* and ending with *na*, the wise one should rest the mind for a single moment upon the head of the sound, light, wind, or radiance.
By means of the practice of the trident, one abandons the earth instantly;
practicing thus for a month, one whirls upon the ground like a wheel. (21)
For a moment it touches the ground, and for a moment the sky;
it utters the howls of jackals and performs writhing movements and slapping sounds.
Whether through the binding of mudrās or by speaking in many ways,
he who is established in samādhi with firm senses shall leave the earth after six months.
The practitioner of yoga stands in the sky at a distance of only one cubit;
he beholds a multitude of yoginīs possessing manifold forms and characteristics.
In a year, the self-disciplined one is born equal to him,
illuminating the quarters with his splendors even as the worlds look on.
Having drawn [the soul] up from the surface of the earth, one becomes the lord of the sky-farers;
this mudrā is called Khageśvarī in the Yoginīmata. (26)
Then, having remained vigilant for three days and nights, the yogin, free from sloth,
should worship Maheśvara at the beginning of the night on the fourth day.
Then, in deep darkness, the wise one, having performed the rite of protection, fixes his mind for a moment between the eyebrows and beholds [the truth]. (28)
Resembling a form of light and seated upon a cross-legged throne,
one who is disciplined in yoga should constantly practice this very application. (29)
Within one month, he perceives whatever object is situated inside the house;
with two months, everything situated outside; and with three months, everything situated within the city.
Within four months, the great yogi perceives the interior of the cavities; within five months, up to the limits of the mandalas; and within six months, he sees the earth as full of holes.
One attains omniscience within a year; there is no doubt about this.
It is established in the pervasive presence of the true being of the assembly of Yoginīs and Siddhas.
One whose self is united with yoga perceives this and becomes equal to Him;
by this very method, one should remain established in the svastika posture. || 33 ||
Having abandoned the various kinds of *bindu*, one should meditate upon the pure form;
by that means, one attains all the previously mentioned supreme fruit. || 34 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Attraction of the Sun," in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara Tantra*.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Therefore, I shall now tell you this supreme secret.
It produces immediate realization for the sake of the yogis' accomplishment of yoga. || 1 ||
Equipped with the previously described ritual placement (nyāsa), one should fix the mind upon the ear in a place free from wind,
or at least very little wind, and devoid of external sounds.
Then, in that state, this yogi hears an unobstructed sound, like that of a perfectly pure bell-metal vessel being struck here again and again. (3)
Having heard this, O Great Goddess, one is liberated from merits and sins;
and there, having fixed his consciousness for six months, he becomes the best among those who know yoga.
He understands even the cries of flocks of birds clearly and without effort; the faculty of hearing from a distance arises within him after one year. (5)
The attainment of the fruits of all desires is accomplished within three years;
what wonder is there that this is achieved without effort?
Alternatively, during the month of Grahaṇa, having placed the sun behind him, equipped with the previously mentioned ritual placement (nyāsa), and leaning slightly against a wall; || 7 ||
One should perceive one's own shadow above the head, unstruck (*anāhata*),
emerging like a column of smoke, by means of the inner self absorbed therein. (8)
To whatever extent one joined in yoga attains identification with that [object], to that same extent a great realization arises within him. (9)
Then, one beholds there a great splendor resembling a flashing ray of light; upon seeing it, even all one's sins are destroyed.
For one who practices this, after a month it spreads everywhere;
he perceives all directions as having a form filled with garlands of flames. (11)
By practicing for six months, the yogi shall attain omniscience;
after one year, having become a divine body, he rejoices for a long time like Śiva.
Now, the [deities] of the various castes, together with their primordial seats and eternal natures, will be described.
Hīṃ, kṣlāṃ, kṣvīṃ, vaṃ, and likewise kṣaṃ are the [seed-syllables] of the pentad in their respective order. || 13 ||
Haṃ, yaṃ, raṃ, laṃ, and likewise vaṃ belong to the other pentad;
ṛṃ, ṝṃ, ḷṃ, ḹṃ, as well as oṃ, auṃ, haḥ, aṃ [are placed] up to the edge of the pericarp.
In the filaments are the syllables ending in *bh*, namely *haṃ*, *hāṃ*, *hiṃ*, *hīṃ*, and *huṃ*;
likewise, on the petals are *hūṃ*, *heṃ*, and *haiṃ*—thus are the Śaktis [placed] according to their respective names.
In the three mandalas, one should fashion the remaining subtle portion of the preta;
this is proclaimed as the syllable *jra* for the tips of the tridents. (15)
p.

155) In all cases where specific mantras for the seats have not been mentioned, one should arrange them in this manner: *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vaṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* are the [six] classes [of mantras]. || 16 ||
In all expiations, one should recite the *mālā* mantra without interruption;
whether it be broken or unbroken, depending on the relative strength or weakness of the transgression.
O Dear One, beginning from a single recitation up to three hundred thousand,
by means of the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇavṛtti), there is nothing higher than that anywhere.

I shall now fully explain the external practice for those who are constantly inclined toward wandering, which bestows the fruit of easy accomplishment within the sacred seats (pīṭha), fields (kṣetra), and other such sites. (19)

One should likewise make the secret [syllable] "nāsākrānta" (the letter *na* conjoined with the nose), which is the Great Breath (*mahāprāṇa*), in the form of a staff (*daṇḍa*) and accompanied by the bindu; this is considered the two-syllabled Vidyā.

O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one who has performed service to her according to the previously mentioned rite and whose mind is serene may wander through the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and other sites for the sake of attaining siddhi; not otherwise.
Having reached that place, one should respectfully surround oneself with mantras and the site with the Vidyā, using a red thread.
But the wise one, with a mind focused in many ways on nothing else, [perceives] both the external and internal;
then, in a certain field there, [he sees] yoginīs of terrifying prowess.
Having assembled, they each bestow their own respective tradition,
O lady of excellent vows, by which [tradition], as soon as it is received, he [attains success].
Having become equal in power to him, he enjoys desired pleasures;
or else, the wise one who has performed service should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Having performed the libation with a tenth part [of the total], one should employ it for minor rites;
merely by reciting this there, it becomes a destroyer of poison. (26)
One should contemplate this [drop] as red within the womb, revolving like a wheel;
or else, by the sequence of going and coming, it is held back at the point of the bindu.
Remaining there, by means of the contraction that shatters the aggregate,
one who is for a moment focused on nothing else can indeed agitate even Urvaśī.

Alternatively, by performing the prescribed service or by reciting [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, one who has been gratified with the fruits of the lotus-gloriousness bestows great fortune. (29)
Even when accomplished by the aforementioned path, the Goddess who abides in the six postures and seats becomes the bestower of all accomplishments for the practitioners of mantra. (30)
Setting aside the ritual for the trident-lotus and the seven [mantras] beginning with Navātman,
the wise one should provide the seat arising from the six [syllables] in every ritual of the cakras.
The great mudrā should be employed along with the worship using the heart-seed syllable.
Now I shall further explain the unsurpassed knowledge of dreams.
Becoming absorbed in that within the heart-cakra, with undistracted mind night after night,
O Great Goddess, whatever one beholds in a dream after a month has passed— || 33 ||
That reality arises for that yogi who is engaged in meditation, provided he remains devoted there with regularity throughout his time. (34)
Then, in the first watch, one's fortune—both auspicious and inauspicious—is determined by one year;
in the second and subsequent watches, it is determined respectively by six months and so forth in sequence. (35)
At the time of dawn, one obtains the fruit within ten days;
this is likewise true whether the rite is performed for others or for oneself, provided it is preceded by a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). (36)
When a certain task has arisen, one should employ the knowledge of the sleeping state;
thus, O Goddess, has been declared the doctrine of the Siddhayogīśvarīmata. (37)
There is no knowledge superior to this within the sphere of Śiva and the rest down to the earth;
he who knows this according to reality is Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt. (38)
"The dust of his feet, when placed upon the head, leads to the pacification of sins.
Having heard this, the Great Goddess attained supreme satisfaction. (39)
Thus he begged for forgiveness, prostrating himself again and again.
In this way, the entire *Mālinīvijayottara* has been narrated to you. (40)
This unsurpassed nectar of yoga was told to me by the Goddess; this great [teaching] must not be disclosed by you to those who are not disciples. (41)
Nor indeed, without having carefully examined the disciples of others, has this been taught in every respect; rather, it is for those whose souls delight in the practice of yoga.
Having obtained this great nectar of knowledge from Kārttikeya, for those who are self-restrained, humble, and whose minds are solely dedicated to Śiva. (43)
"Having practiced yoga, the sages have attained supreme perfection.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara Tantra. 23.
And thus concludes this great tantra named the Mālinīvijayottara.
By the command of the illustrious King Pratāpa, and for the delight of the virtuous,
this has been prepared and published by Madhusūdana Kaula.
May this be offered unto Śrī Sāmbaśiva.
